item.title: Gamification of mathematics off the charts
item.description: How mathematicians can benefit without undermining professional norms and values
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
A dilemma

The 2025 article

Geometric Langlands in positive characteristic from characteristic zero

by Gaitsgory and Raskin is the main application to number theory of the monumental solution of the (categorical, unramified) geometric Langlands conjecture, itself due directly to Gaitsgory and Raskin and seven named collaborators, and indirectly to several generations of mathematicians, all rooted in Vladimir Drinfel’d’s work of the 1970s and 1980s. My recent paper with Beuzart-Plessis and Thorne makes critical use of one of the main results of the 2025 article: the fact that at most one everywhere unramified automorphic representation of a reductive group G over a global function field over a finite field k has a given irreducible global Galois parameter, under the construction due to Vincent Lafforgue. The Gaitsgory-Raskin result is valid under mild restrictions on the characteristic of k, and our result has slightly stronger restrictions, as well as a dependence on a version of the stable trace formula for function fields that has not yet been proven. These restrictions are irrelevant to the dilemma I am about to describe.

Gaitsgory and Raskin point out in their introduction that they

have not solved the most mysterious part of the Langlands conjecture,

namely that there is exactly one everywhere unramified automorphic representation of G with a given irreducible global Galois parameter. Such a result would represent a complete solution of the unramified Langlands conjecture for function fields. And just such a result has been announced in the OpenAI repository released on October 6.1 I have not tried to read the claimed solution and I am waiting to hear what, if anything, the authors have been able to extract from it.

My paper with Beuzart-Plessis and Thorne contains a remark to the effect that, assuming the solution of this “most mysterious part of the Langlands conjecture” for everywhere unramified parameters, our methods could be extended to prove the same “most mysterious part” for everywhere finitely ramified parameters, conditionally as in our paper. Various strategies would then be available to extend the result to all parameters, and specialists would undoubtedly enjoy spending a few years wrapping up the problem and developing methods and insights that can then be applied much more broadly to problems in geometry and number theory.2

But to use any of the results in the OpenAI repository would be to validate not only the results but the means by which they were obtained and announced, thus contributing to the undermining of the norms and functioning that the existing mathematical community has established over decades, norms themselves based on the evolution of mathematical practice since the very beginning of human civilization.

Fortunately, Terry Tao’s 2026 ICM lecture includes a “rule of thumb” that can be used as the basis of a solution, if the mathematical community can bring itself to accept it.

Tao’s rule of thumb

When I heard Tao’s lecture I assumed, and probably most of his audience assumed, that he was thinking of individual authors of AI-generated texts, human beings who could be invited to a physical or virtual location to present a “clear, expert-level talk.” No one in the audience anticipated the deluge of AI-generated texts, based on a Grand Theft of the mathematical literature of unprecedented scope, the “greatest math heist in history,” with no identifiable authors, that was dumped on the mathematical landscape on October 6.

Elsewhere I will argue that the rule stated on Tao’s slide both authorizes us and compels us to treat this deluge as a downpour of fertilizer, freely available for the taking by the less squeamish members of our community, with any nutrients eventually to be incorporated in papers meeting Tao’s rule of thumb and acknowledged — if at all — as “AI assistance.” I would have no trouble citing such a paper, especially if it has previously been validated by Gaitsgory and Raskin, who are the most directly concerned by the result.

This would resolve my personal dilemma, but it would not provide a meaningful answer to a different concern, which is that the frontier labs may, just barely, be able to turn pillaging mathematics into a profitable business model.

Subscribe now

Gamification as market niche

In their interesting dialogue — that nevertheless concedes far too much to a functionalist model of mathematics as a branch of the market economy that is diametrically opposed to the model I am trying to promote of mathematics as gift economy — Thomas Koberda and Alex Kontorovich, in the process of elaborating a “Dialectical Theorem” that describes an optimistic future for PhD students in mathematics, mention in passing the emergence of a new subculture around the Grand Theft of mathematics:

Now amateurs type “do a brkthru” [internet subculture slang for prompting AI to prove a breakthrough result] and actually get one!3

Now expand this subculture to the scope of the international video game industry. Estimates of its size vary widely but are all in the hundreds of billions of dollars, with some estimates approaching $600 billion as early as this year. Suppose OpenAI and Anthropic, or whichever of the two survives until 2030, manages to tap even a fraction of this potential market, offering champion gamers bespoke prompts to claim their very own mathematical brkthrus, theorems, like lunar craters or galaxies at the fringe of the visible universe, eternally bearing their own names, that mathematicians (human or artificial) will be compelled to cite.

It’s a long shot, but this may be just the killer app the industry needs to remain afloat long enough to make the transition to the military contracts that have always already been their destiny.

Advice from Andrea Bartz of Bartz vs. Anthropic

Copied from Graham Lovelace’s Substack Charting GenAI4

What’s the one thing you’d like people to take away from this interview, from your experience?

So here in the US, we keep hearing about how AI is inevitable and just shut up and take it. There’s no going back. It’s not like you need to use this because we have decided that you will be using this. And I just want people to understand that AI isn’t this unstoppable tsunami just because the AI companies say it is. It’s not inevitable. We still have a choice. If little me, a mid-list writer In Brooklyn, New York can stand up against the Goliath of this $900 billion company and come out victorious. That means that lots of other creators can take similar stands.

And so I hope that this settlement reminds people that They can push back, right? And that can be in big ways, like through the legal system, which I’m sure is very different in every country. That can also be in your own community, within your own friend groups. At minimum, I hope that it really looks like refusing to use generative AI yourself and having those conversations with other people. There’s a wonderful website called AIresistlist.org that just sort of compiles some different grassroots organizations that are resisting AI in different ways. And, you know, I always say action is the antidote to anxiety.

Leave a comment

1

The task of locating this announcement in the repository is left to the intrepid reader.

2

I have seen a proposal to reach the same conclusion based on a fascinating and wildly different strategy, but given the current state of surveillance of mathematical communications by hostile forces the authors of this proposal are wisely not sharing it with the community.

3

Google Gemini just told me:

No, "brkthru" is not internet slang for using AI to achieve breakthrough results in mathematics

For the same of argument, I will assume — and I have no reason to doubt — that the authors are better informed than Gemini.

4

“Creatives must avoid AI, says author who took on Big Tech and won.” Andrea Bartz tells the Creators Emergency Summit ‘there’s no ethical way to use gen AI’.

Full disclosure: My two books with Princeton University Press are covered by the Anthropic settlement.

item.title: Now all mathematicians can be Mechanical Turks
item.description: But we can also choose not to be
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
There was brief speculation at the philosophy conference I’m now attending, entitled “Mathematical Proof in the Age of AI,” that OpenAI released its “722 manuscripts organized into 372 families” on the eve of the conference precisely in order to create havoc in the minds of the assembled philosophers and mathematicians, but this hypothesis was quickly discarded. Nevertheless, as you can imagine, it was impossible to avoid talking about the contents of the Github repository and its “Implications of the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Mathematical Research,” to quote the conference’s subtitle. It didn’t take long for everyone here to agree with the understatement in the New York Times article: Although OpenAI claimed to have “have drawn on the[] advice [of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence] and public recommendations⁠ to inform how we release these results,”

OpenAI… seems to be less interested in a key recommendation of the advisory board, that the A.I. companies should stop testing their proprietary models on advanced mathematical problems. “We want to state clearly from the start: we do not endorse this practice,” the advisory board wrote on Sept. 29.

It’s just another episode in the long series of obfuscations and broken promises, starting with its name, that have made OpenAI a byword for mendacity.

Contemplating OpenAI’s pillaging of the mathematical commons from my vantage point on the Norwegian coast, it’s hard not to think of the Viking sack of Lindisfarne and other sites along the British and French coasts.

This sentence from an arXiv post could probably be duplicated dozens if not hundreds of times:

The result is also contained in a paper… released by OpenAI on October 6, 2026, in which the proof strategy and specific choices of notation are identical to a preliminary version of the present paper that was uploaded to ChatGPT on September 8, 2026.

My own paper with Ciubotaru was used in a paper purporting to prove a strengthening of our main result — and also of the main result of joint work with Gaitsgory and Lafforgue announced in Sam Raskin’s ICM talk. Raskin’s paper was not cited, while mine with Ciubotaru was cited in its arXiv version. All readers need to know about this is that Ciubotaru and I posted our preprint on arXiv with a Creative Common non-commercial use license, as did the authors of at least 88 of the other papers cited in the OpenAI repository. Since these papers were used to train OpenAI’s commercial models, and were cited in the paper dump that served as a backdrop to OpenAI’s ongoing marketing operation, I contend that OpenAI violated our rights as authors.

But that’s hardly the worst of OpenAI’s offenses. Two of the short reactions just published on the Proofs and Prompts website point to the precise form of OpenAI’s disruption of international mathematics:

I do not wish to be part of what in some cases would amount to free publicity and free refereeing for OpenAI, contributing to the false narrative being pushed that this company is now actively collaborating with the mathematical community. A second reason is that in organising ourselves in such a way and at such a scale, we implicitly accept this new division of labour, where proof-production can become completely decoupled from any form of proof-comprehension, and where this dehumanized proof-production process becomes increasingly tied with an arms race for computing resources.

(Alexandre Martin)

They can simply release multiple 100+ page papers claiming to have solved this or that problem, often with redundant arguments, unclear logical structure, multiple dead ends, and strange or unsettling terminology — in other words, slop. And we are then expected to go through it, check it, clean it up, simplify it, and explain what is actually going on.

This comes at a considerable cost to us in terms of time and effort, while they can simply move on and slop-bulldoze the next conjecture. And, of course, the credit remains theirs. In some sense, we are willingly contributing to our own demise.

I think the paradigm has to shift. We should apply to AI-generated mathematical announcements the same standards of rigour, clarity, and exposition that we demand from human-generated papers. Do you want the approval of the mathematical community? A badge of legitimacy? Then give us something that is actually readable and verifiable. If not, we should simply ignore it.

In other words, I do not think that we, as a community, should spend our time cleaning up their mess in order to increase someone else’s commercial revenues.

(Enrico Fatighenti)

In other words, OpenAI expects the mathematical community to set aside its own priorities and to devote its time and energy to verifying and explicating OpenAI’s 722 papers, placing mathematicians in the subordinate position relative to the tech industry of the Mechanical Turks, a development I anticipated just over a year ago.

Even to read the OpenAI papers relevant to my field in search of useful new ideas, without committing time to refining their arguments or correcting their errors, would amount to consenting to “take my assigned slot as Mechanical Turk,” as I wrote last year.1 Being paid for the service would not make it more acceptable, quite the contrary. As I wrote yesterday in response to a journalist’s question:

A mathematician who behaved in this way [i.e., like OpenAI] would be considered unwelcome in the community. So why would self-respecting specialists want to help them polish their results, or to associate with them in any way?

On the other hand, simply ignoring these papers, as Enrico Fatighenti suggests, is not a viable individual strategy. Many of the reactions published on Proofs and Prompts and elsewhere call for a collective response. Whether the mathematical community can unite around such a response, and what form it will take, remains to be seen.

Leave a comment

1

(Added November 1) Asaf Karagila’s explanation, which I just discovered, of why he will not be offering Sam Altman a bottle of whisky, even though the OpenAI repository contains an “announcement that the Partition Principle does not imply the Axiom of Choice,” and although Karagila had promised just such a reward to anyone who solved the problem, makes the same point.

item.title: The essay on the Navier-Stokes story that everyone should read
item.description: Alexander Gamburd sets a very high bar
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
Alexander Gamburd circulated the first version of his essay “The Siren Call of Silicon Leviathan” in mid-September, acknowledging with implicit regret that it was “probably way too long to be posted (e.g. on your substack).” An even longer version — 26 pages, plus an additional 40 pages of endnotes! — has now been posted on arXiv. Everyone who has an opinion about the the subject of this newsletter should read it. It is not light reading, especially if you decide (as I recommend) not to skip the endnotes, but to my mind it is one of the two most thoughtful essays anyone has written to draw out the implications of AI for mathematics, the other one being “The fall of the theorem economy” by David Bessis.

Gamburd argues, with ingenious metaphors and drawing on an astounding range of references,1 that “Mathematics was central to the enlightenment” because it created “knowledge that compels assent without appeal to authority, that is the same for the peasant and the prince, that any human being with patience may verify.” This argument is developed in the excerpt copied below. The flip side is that the application of AI to mathematics undoes the work of the enlightenment:

Mathematics once more contains truths that exceed all the ability of human reason and are held on authority; the authority is the Lean proof checker and the corporation that owns the prover; the clergy are those who can put questions to the prover and interpret what it returns, the corporation’s mathematicians first; the language the laity cannot read is not Latin but Lean.

(To avoid misattribution, I have chosen to reproduce passages from Gamburd’s text in blue, here and below.) Gamburd distinguishes demonstration from certificate: the corporations, possessed of “subhuman superintelligence,” provide the latter but only a humanly comprehensible proof counts as a demonstation.

A certificate is a document: it informs us, reliably, that a monument exists, and that is all. The Lean proof of 8 September is a document 616,000 lines long about a monument no one has visited. We may believe the document. But a civilization whose knowledge consists of documents about monuments it does not visit has ceased, on Panofsky’s definition and on Hobbes’s, to be a humanist civilization, whatever the state of its certainties.

But press releases about mathematics are now central to the prestige of the frontier labs, and Gamburd concludes that this gives mathematics a surprising power in the last instance:

The [mathematical] community’s sword is the one this essay has already drawn, acceptance withheld; it is a bloodless sword, and it is the only one the Leviathans2 cannot forge for themselves, since it is the thing they compete for.

                                     The history of ideas began a long time ago

When the panelists at the Heidelberg Laureate Forum were asked “What general career advice would you give to a beginning Ph.D. student, in view of AI?,” my answer included the following two items:

  • study philosophy to avoid being swayed by spurious arguments and sensationalist predictions, all of which misrepresent the nature and aims of mathematics as a social practice;

  • study social science and the humanities so you can recognize how language is used to discourage resistance; note in particular the similarities between the rhetoric about the inevitability of an AI takeover of mathematics and the 19th century rhetoric of progress that accompanied colonialism.

I should have added that issues very much like those raised by the arrival of AI in mathematics have been addressed repeatedly in the long history of reflection upon the human condition. Whether or not you agree with Gamburd’s text, its great merit is to demonstrate how the the debate can be clarified — enlightened — by restoring it to its proper place as a chapter in the history of ideas.

For example, Po-Shen Loh’s essay “Why Do We Need Human Mathematicians Anymore?” published on the author’s blog and as a guest post on Terence Tao’s (widely-read) blog, is an admirable attempt to answer the question in the title. But it makes the mistake, all too common when mathematicians grapple with ethical or epistemological or aesthetic questions, of forgetting that similar questions have occupied human minds, in every literate culture, for thousands of years.

And whether or not Daniel Litt is correct when he claims that

As we think about how to reshape our profession, it’s important to understand that, whether one likes it or not, it’s impossible to stop people, amateur or professional, from pushing a button to produce mathematics. The idea that we will persuade people not to play around with math, or that we will be able to “reserve” problems for graduate students, is just not realistic.

he owes it to his readers to remember that the question — whether or not human beings are so incorrigible that it is impossible to stop some of them from defying community norms — has been the subject of energetic and extensive reflection, notably reflection on how to create a stable form of government that respects accepted principles of justice. One need look no further than the Federalist Papers 6, in which Alexander Hamilton asked

Has it not… invariably been found that momentary passions, and immediate interest, have a more active and imperious control over human conduct than general or remote considerations of policy, utility or justice?

or the Federalist Papers 51, with James Madison’s famous line:

If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary.

Gamburd’s erudition is exceptional, but everyone who wants to share their sensible ideas should first remind themselves that it is almost certain that generations of thinkers have come up repeatedly with the same ideas, and others have refuted them, and that contributing to a debate on pressing issues means acknowledging what these past generations have contributed and debating them as well.3

Subscribe now

             Section I of Gamburd’s essay:  Mathematics and the Enlightenment

Mathematics was central to the Enlightenment, which took off as a fledgling startup with the Principia, the demonstration that a handful of propositions governed the apple and the moon alike: Fontenelle drew the moral that l’esprit géométrique was not so attached to geometry that it could not be carried into other kinds of knowledge. D’Alembert made the mathematical sciences the only ones “marked with the seal of evidence” and graded every other discipline by its distance from them; Kant held that a doctrine of nature contained exactly as much science as it contained mathematics; and Condorcet proposed a mathématique sociale.

But the deepest of mathematics’ services to the Enlightenment unicorn—the one that yielded spectacular returns indeed—was neither doctrinal nor methodological. Mathematics was the proof of concept, the demonstration that what the Enlightenment wanted was possible at all: knowledge that compels assent without appeal to authority, that is the same for the peasant and the prince, that any human being with patience may verify. It did not have to be invented by the founders; it already existed, for a geometrical demonstration is a truth that owes nothing to whoever asserts it. Locke recommended mathematics “not so much to make them mathe- maticians as to make them reasonable creatures,” and the phrase tells us what a reasonable creature was: someone who would not take the forty-seventh proposition on Euclid’s word, but would follow it back until the impossible became necessary. There were no mysteries in Euclid beyond the reach of human reason; that was the point the Enlightenment made of Euclid. Mathematics was, strictly speaking, not the Enlightenment’s proof of concept but its existence proof: it did not show that autonomous reason might work; it exhibited an instance. That is why one might say that the Enlightenment—in effect—bound itself to the mast of its firstborn, and why the ship of mathematics entering thoroughly turbulent waters threatens the Enlightenment project, potentially in its totality.

The converse is less familiar but no less pertinent: it was the Enlightenment that made math- ematics as we now know it. Until the Enlightenment the subject was, at its frontier, a private and often a courtly art. Tartaglia surrendered the solution of the cubic to Cardano only un- der oath; Newton sent the method of fluxions to Leibniz as an anagram; the Bernoullis issued challenge problems as one issues a challenge to a duel; a result was property, and property was defended by concealment. The Enlightenment turned that private possession into pub- lic reason. The academies and the journals made publication rather than possession the act by which a result came into existence; priority went to whoever printed first; credit attached to a name anyone could cite; the demonstration was addressed to an anonymous reader presumed competent. André Weil, opening the Euler chapter of his history of number theory, marks the change. Until the latter part of the seventeenth century mathematics “had sometimes bestowed high reputation upon its adepts but had seldom provided them with the means to social ad- vancement and honorable employment,” and its results traveled through “a private network of informants”; then, “by the time of Euler’s birth in 1707, a radical change had taken place,” and “scientific life, by the turn of the century, had acquired a structure not too different from what we witness to-day.” Euler wrote eight hundred papers to be read, and the Letters to a German Princess—no less than Descartes’s letters to Elisabeth of Bohemia a century before— to be followed by a princess. The same century made mathematics an instrument of social advancement—the École Polytechnique admitted by examination, and Fourier the tailor’s son, d’Alembert the foundling and Monge the pedlar’s son had shown what the subject could do for those without high birth, though not yet for those without the right sex, for Sophie Germain followed Lagrange’s course there from its lecture notes under a man’s name—and it fixed the modern standard of rigor. Cauchy’s Cours d’analyse of 1821 was a Polytechnique course, and Grabiner has argued that its rigor was in part a consequence of teaching: a working analyst could rely on a trained sense of when a series converged or a limit existed, but that sense cannot be lectured to a hall of students, and what can be lectured is a definition that decides every case and a proof that uses nothing else. Rigor is tact made teachable, and the École had to teach. Lagrange, lecturing at the same school a generation earlier, had founded the calculus on power series in the Théorie des fonctions analytiques; Cauchy’s limits replaced them.

The norms of the mathematics we practice—preprints accessible to all, credit by citation, publication necessitating refereeing by peers, and thereby (and only thus) establishing priority (a practice given its definitive modern form by Lamb’s teacher Stokes, during thirty-one years as Secretary of the Royal Society and editor of its Transactions), understanding as the end and proof as the means—are not artifacts of lex naturalis but Enlightenment institutions. Publication used to discharge three functions at once—announcing a result, identifying its contributors, and demonstrating understanding—which had never needed to be distinguished, because for three centuries the capability of producing a deep theorem was vested in a human mind that had understood it. The mathematical community is a tiny, open, unarmed and (by and large) honorable republic—a province of what d’Alembert called the Republic of Letters—that publishes everything in advance, without promise of remuneration; not from naïveté, but because its whole constitution—as well as its raison d’être—was the abolition of walls.

This two-edged contention—that mathematics was the Enlightenment’s existence proof of concept, and that the Enlightenment was the maker of mathematics as we now know it—goes a long way towards explaining why the decisive engagement between the frontier models and the learned world took place in mathematics rather than in ________, where the money is. A theorem in Lean either passes the proof checker or does not, so mathematics is the one irre- placeably consequential domain of human knowledge in which a machine can be told, at scale and without a human judge, whether it has succeeded: in the trainers’ own jargon, the do- main of verifiable rewards, the verdict that elsewhere must be bought from human graders being here supplied by the proof checker at no cost; and mathematics is transacted entirely in text, so its whole frontier is reachable through nothing but tokens (the esprit géométrique thereby submerged). But the deepest reason is the Enlightenment’s own doing: it had agreed to regard mathematics as reason’s home, and a machine that computes proves its claim to reason most convincingly there. From Turing’s chess to Go to the IMO, the proxies for machine intelligence have been formal games, and mathematics is perceived as the oldest of them, the one Hobbes meant by “Reckoning.” When the machines began to solve olympiad problems, Jacob Tsimerman put a question to his Doktorvater, Peter Sarnak, who had observed that this told more about the competitions than about the machines: “What level does the AI need to perform at before you take it seriously? What would it need to do? When would you change your mind?” This essay attempts to unravel the answer that 8 September appears to have given. The Millennium million is small change, and so is whatever was spent to claim it; what really was at stake was the relative standing of the two powers that contend for the title of this essay, and the episode was less about advancing mathematics than about being seen to have done so. To be seen to do mathematics is to be seen to think. One may view the open literature of this section as a commons, and the frontier models as its enclosure. The first consequence is already visible: that mathematicians may come to guard their work in order to keep it from being taken. That is the road back to Tartaglia, and a Middle Ages in reverse—Panofsky’s phrase from my epigraph, whose meaning section IV takes up—is likely to affect the sociology of the subject before reaching its epistemology. Simone Weil held that the three monsters of contemporary civilization are “Money, mechanisation, algebra,” and the Silicon Leviathan is the point at which the three become one body. The Leviathan of Job lived in one of the four classical elements. The Silicon Leviathan lives in a fifth, and Weil put it first on her list.

                                                             Bloodless swords

Gamburd’s suggestion that the mathematical community could withhold its acceptance of the results issued by the AI labs — meaning refusing to acknowledge them as valid contributions to the mathematical literature, was anticipated by Terence Tao’s introduction of the notion of canonicalization in his public lecture at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia. Tao may or may not have borrowed the word from computer science but he gives it a precise meaning in the text based on his lecture:

Key results should ultimately become part of the definitive textbooks and reference material of their subject, in the form in which they are taught to the next generation of students. This process of canonicalization — in which a result is restated in its natural generality, given its right proof rather than its first proof, connected to its neighbors, and absorbed into the standard toolkit — is the slowest stage of all. It requires broad, deliberative consensus, and it is the stage least amenable to optimization by AI tools. It is also, in my view, the most valuable part of the entire process.

More recently, Stepan Nesterov, a graduate student at Stanford, proposed a definition of proof on the site Proofs and Prompts that, suitably interpreted,4 looks like the only one compatible with canonicalization, and that corresponds to what working mathematicians have meant in practice by proof, until formalization became fashionable:

Definition. A mathematical proof is a text in natural language which explains to a person sufficiently well-trained in mathematics why a certain statement is correct. A statement is mathematically proven, if there is a mathematical proof which is accepted to be correct by sufficiently many well-respected members of the mathematical community.

More officially, the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), which “came together after OpenAI approached some of its members about establishing an external advisory board” but chose instead to remain strictly independent of the industry, issued its first guidelines yesterday for “responsible release of AI-generated mathematics.” The nine members of AGMAI begin by making clear that

we do not endorse [what the industry is doing], and we ask [AI labs] to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.

But since they know the industry will continue doing so anyway, they state conditions under which AI-generated mathematics might be considered compatible with community norms. Moreover, they ask the labs “to make an appropriate [financial] contribution to fulfilling their responsibility towards the development of human understanding of their AI output,” although they stipulate that “acceptance of such support by the mathematical community would not be conferring legitimacy on the practices of the AI labs.” This group of mathematicians, at least, is unwilling to forge the sword for which the Leviathans compete.

Leave a comment

1

Stretching from Plato, Cicero, Augustine, and the Book of Job, up to Dario Amodei and Marc Andreessen, with special attention to Hobbes, the Nazi jurist Carl Schmitt, the art historian Erwin Panofsky, and the Dialectic of Enlightenment of Horkheimer and Adorno; with cameos by Homer, Auden, Bulgakov, and Antonioni; plus many, many mathematicians from the time of D’Alembert and Euler (and both Navier and Stokes) to the present.

2

by which he means OpenAI and Anthropic

3

The next step is to use one’s reason and rudimentary knowledge of history to guess where these debates took place; this was the strategy that led me to the quotations from the Federalist Papers, but I could just as well have consulted the European thinkers of the Enlightenment, or the annals of the revolutions of 1848.

4

All of these suggestions are necessarily ambiguous, by the very nature of community.

item.title: The real story, and the official story
item.description: Reasons for optimism
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
On the morning of September 8 I was on the verge of finishing and publishing a post with this title and most of the content below when I woke to a message advising me to read what Tristan Buckmaster had published on Mastodon a few hours earlier. Thus I found myself obliged to put together a report on the Navier-Stokes story in haste. Within two days that post had become the most widely viewed of anything I had written during the five years since I started this newsletter. As of today the number of views has reached more than 19000, more than double its nearest competitor, which as it happens also concerns a scandal involving OpenAI. One is led to suspect that hostility to OpenAI is widespread among readers of newsletters like this one.

So many articles have appeared in various press outlets, large and small, in response to the OpenAI announcement and Buckmaster’s reaction, that many or most of my readers will already have heard of Proofs and Prompts, of the “Severe misalignment” essay signed by 25 Fields Medalists, and of the Association for Human Mathematics. Nevertheless, for the same of completeness, and because the post below was nearly finished when its publication had to be postponed, I am publishing it now. I was unable to publish it immediately because I was involved in some of the fallout from the Navier-Stokes story. For example, I was quoted in the article Science magazine devoted to the story that very same day, and I stand by what I said:

“I certainly don’t expect the industry to continue to spend millions of dollars to solve problems in mathematics, because there is no profit in it,” Columbia University mathematician Michael Harris wrote in an email to Science. But he worries the highly publicized achievement will be “extremely damaging to mathematics; it convinces decision makers that human mathematicians are obsolete, and it convinces young people that their passion for mathematics has no future.”

Moreover, the inevitable focus on Navier-Stokes forced me to rethink what I was going to say at the panel to which I was invited at the Heidelberg Laureate Forum, alongside Peter Scholze, Geordie Williamson, and Jacob Tsimerman, on the inevitable topic AI in mathematical research.1 During the three days I spent in Heidelberg I was interviewed by journalists from three different countries. At the conference in Paris for the 100th birthday of Jean-Pierre Serre, all the conversations were about AI, mostly taking the Navier-Stokes story as starting point, although very few of those attending the conference were in any way professionally involved with the question.

Now I have a few minutes to finish the delayed post. With luck I will be able to include everything I had been planning to say before lights out. Otherwise it will have to wait until the post after next; my very next post will consist of the slides from a talk for philosophers, about the Ramanujan Conjecture, inspired by Peter Sarnak’s AlphaZero test.

       The question “who speaks for mathematics?” has been answered, beautifully

For nearly three weeks2 I have been fuming over a Washington Post article that Google tags as

Fuming, but fortunately not willing to interrupt my vacation, because at the same time I was able to watch the website proofsandprompts.com blossom, incredibly, into exactly what mathematics needs, and at just the right time.

The editors (or hosts?) announce on their “About” page that they subscribe to the Leiden Declaration. As for the purpose of the site, I’ll let them speak for themselves:

…this is a blog written by mathematicians, for mathematicians, where people can think aloud about how these tools are changing mathematical practice, without having to justify the premise or dumb down the stakes, without being confined to benchmarks and product announcements, all in a common place to facilitate a fruitful exchange of ideas.

We’re especially interested in voices that don’t usually get a platform for this kind of reflection, that can come here without having to set up and maintain a personal blog. Senior researchers with an established audience are welcome, but so are PhD students still forming an opinion, mathematicians who’ve tried these tools and been unimpressed, and those who haven’t touched them at all and want to say why. We think the range of reactions — enthusiasm, indifference, anxiety, contempt, curiosity — is itself part of the record worth keeping.

The 28th post was published this morning,3 exactly one month after the first. The list of contributors counts long established mathematicians, including two Fields Medalists, as well as current graduate students, and pretty much everything in between. Colleagues preferred by the news media — for example, those with the kind of name recognition that qualifies them for crossword clues — receive no special privilege. Every one of the posts I have read — and I have read most of them4 — is thoughtful, sincere, frank, and entirely lacking in the kind of arrogance, dismissiveness, or condescension that characterizes too much of the public debate about AI, whatever the context. In other words, it is at the opposite end of the discursive universe from the miasma of Twitter, where a snide comment like this one represents the upper limit of rhetorical respect for those with whom one disagrees.

And there are disagreements on proofsandprompts.com! The hosts (or moderators?) themselves all cite extensive experience with AI or Lean or both, and can’t be accused of hostility to technology. But they write

We welcome sharp criticism, disagreement, and strong opinions, including about labs, institutions, and this blog. That is much of the point.

and draw the line at

posts that attack or demean people on the basis of race, ethnicity, religion, gender, sexual orientation, disability, or nationality, that condone violence or self-harm, or that are posted in bad faith to provoke rather than to discuss.

Some of the essays are highly critical of AI, even entertaining the option of banning AI-generated mathematics outright. Other essays urge mathematicians to embrace the possibilities offered by the technology. Some posts have been written specifically in order to rebut points made in earlier posts. There have been posts about teaching, about writing, about the profession, and about the different needs of pure and applied mathematicians. What I have not seen, and don’t expect to see, are spurious reasoning, unmotivated assertions, or ad hominem attacks.

As far as I know the existence of such a forum for debate among mathematicians is unprecedented. Journals of professional associations5 have long provided curated platforms for debate of timely or controversial topics as well as sections for letters to the editor; but space in these journals is limited and turnaround time was long. MathOverflow states explicitly that it “is not a discussion forum” and reddit hardly lends itself to extended arguments.

The question I asked back in April — “Who speaks for mathematics?” — has now been answered. One link away and the answer will be on your screen. This is the real story of AI and mathematics, and journalists are advised to take note.

Subscribe now

                                                    Beyond the Leiden Declaration

And so are their editors. The official story, in contrast to the real story, of an increasing alignment of mathematics with the interests of the AI industry, and an increasing marginalization of those who refuse this alignment, is still being promoted by ill-informed or unscrupulous editors.

I’ll soon get to a particularly egregious recent example. But first, it is a duty as well as a pleasure to draw your attention to a brand new initiative, also part of the real story, driven by (among others) some of the people mentioned in my last post. The Association for Human Mathematics (AHM) aims to “maintain the independence of the mathematical community from the encroachment of corporate interest.” If this sentence looks familiar, it may be because you read it at the very top of this post. Other sentences in the 23 lines of the AHM’s membership statement, I’m pleased to say, address the role of the AI industry in a way very similar to what I have been writing for the last five years.

The AHM is a membership organization, and all members have to make a commitment to respect the following two rules:

1. Members commit to not working with commercial AI companies by providing technical labor, mathematical knowledge, consultation, or publicity.

2. Members commit to not publishing mathematical texts (including papers, reviews, referee reports, lecture notes, teaching materials, and books) generated by AI models. Members only publish their own writing, as opposed to outputs of AI tools. We affirm that mathematical writing should have human authorship.

Members also have the option of making the stronger commitment to joining the AI-free caucus (which some colleagues have taken to calling “the vegans”):

3. Members of the AI-free caucus do not use AI models in a research capacity. Members of this caucus engage in core mathematical activities, such as finding proofs, exploring examples, and posing research questions, without prompting Al tools.

Quite a few of the 645 members have taken this pledge. I am not in fact using AI models in my research, and don’t anticipate doing so in the foreseeable future, but I have no objection in principle to homemade machine learning tools, like the one Thomas Lanard and Alberto Mínguez designed in the project mentioned here in order to detect patterns in representation theory, nor to possible future AI resources made available by a hypothetical public authority that is not beholden to commercial interests, as proposed explicitly in one of the points in the Leiden Declaration. So I have not committed to point 3. 

                                     The “Severe Misalignment” statement

Rounding out my review of the real story, for now, is the declaration published three days after the Navier-Stokes announcement — on the 25th anniversary of the attack on the Twin Towers in New York City! — and signed by 25 Fields medalists. The statement makes no explicit reference to Navier-Stokes, but it’s hard not to assume that OpenAI’s exploitation of the story wasn’t the catalyst for many or most of the signatories.

The text is short and deserves to be read in full.6 The first paragraph already sets the tone:

Over the last few months, the mathematical capabilities of LLMs have improved dramatically, to the point that they can solve major outstanding problems in many fields of mathematics. However, the push by AI companies to solve mathematical problems as a benchmark is detrimental to the science of mathematics, and to the mathematical community. The goals of the AI companies and the goals of the mathematical community are severely misaligned. We see these as part of broader alignment issues impacting other scientific and creative professions, as well as the whole of society.

A French translation of this declaration was published in Le Monde, also on September 11. One week later, Le Monde published a story reporting on “an unprecedented crisis among mathematicians” provoked by AI, mentioning Proofs and Prompts, and AHM, and the fact that the Fields medalists’ statement had by then been endorsed by more than 7400 people.7

The Le Monde journalist added an interesting observation (my translation):

…mathematicians undoubtedly belong to the only discipline that can take pride in resembling an international community.

This international community now counts 4100 signatories of the Leiden declaration, 645 members of the Association for Human Mathematics, and 7700 endorsers8 of the “Severe Misalignment” statement. That is the real story and Le Monde’s reporter is to be applauded for telling it. The same cannot be said of most of his fellow journalists. The remainder of this post is devoted to an especially offensive version of the official story, the one the industry wants consumers of the media to believe. 

                        The official story:  dismay and despair in 50+ column inches

An alternative which has planted dismay and despair in every heart that palpitates in that [Cherokee] nation…9

I’m told about 40 mathematicians were flown out to San Francisco in early August, shortly after the International Congress in Philadelphia, for a one-day “summit.” The purpose of the summit, according to the one news report I’ve seen about the meeting, was

an existential question: What will be left for human math experts to do if artificial intelligence soon leaves them all behind?

This news report was published in the Washington Post; it’s the “what’s left for humans” article cited near the top of the post you are currently reading. One week earlier, the journalist had written to ask me for an interview, introducing herself as “a reporter at the Washington Post working on a story trying to take stock of all these new AI-generated/assisted results in mathematics.” When the article came out I wrote to thank her for not quoting me “because the article, starting with the title, is just one more example of what Shane Kelly called ‘a large scale advertising campaign by AI companies competing for market monopoly,’ in a footnote to his recent paper.”10

In my most recent post, I wrote that

The article was awful not because of how it was written but because of what it reveals: that the AI industry is using prominent mathematicians as extras in a marketing operation masquerading as a drama, and that even the most sophisticated among the mathematicians play their roles, naively imagining that the drama is about them.

If the official story is not really about mathematicians, then what is it about? My response to a question at the Heidelberg panel, about the media portrayal of mathematics in connection with AI, suggests it’s all about the psychology of news editors:

Headlines like “The summer AI ate math” (Scientific American) or “If AI can do math, what’s the point of mathematicians?” (Scientific American) or “This may be the first academic profession to see its work taken over by AI” (Washington Post) are such a violent misrepresentation of the human practice of mathematics that one wonders whether they are not a form of belated revenge editors are taking against their math teachers.

I don’t actually believe this answer, however. In the official story mathematicians despair upon encountering the real heroes. We have seen this story before. The earliest readers of Silicon Reckoner even saw the picture of this story, nearly five years ago. The hero is “Progress,” in the shape of a gigantic floating white woman, and the Native Americans, who are shown being literally blown away (along with the buffalo), figure as collateral damage. The epigraph to this section comes from one of numerous documents published in the 19th century in the wake of the dispossession of the indigenous population by the westward expansion of the United States.

There are many ways to tell the story of colonialism. In July 2025 the Department of Homeland Security went so far as to revive the John Gast painting “American Progress,” pictured in my newsletter a year before the release of ChatGPT, as an expression of pride in the colonial project, in the 19th century, and by implication today as well. That’s the version of the story Silicon Valley broadcasts, with the help of the media, each time it announces another advance in its ongoing hostile takeover of mathematics.

But the story of colonialism can also be framed as regret for what is being lost, highlighting the “dismay and despair” of one native tribe after another, as in all those 19th century reports. The Washington Post article unsurprisingly gives OpenAI’s Sébastien Bubeck the last word. “We have to put the people, the human, the mathematicians first,” he says, just after suggesting that this may require the human, like the buffalo in Gast’s painting, to scale back their ambitions. “[M]aybe the field should consider pivoting to AI safety,” Bubeck muses — to move to the reservations Silicon Valley has set aside for them and to go to work for the corporations responsible for their displacement. Who would refuse such an offer?

The one mistake that must not be made is to imagine that the official story is about the colonized. The official story is always about the powerful. That’s why it’s so important to celebrate the many mathematicians who are making it their project to publish the real story.

Leave a comment

1

You can watch it on YouTube and decide for yourself who among the panelists was most convincing, and who made the best jokes.

2

Make that five weeks.

3

That was written on September 8. By now (September 21) there have been 50 posts.

4

That was written more than two weeks ago. By now so much has been written on the platform that I have been unable to keep up. But I try.

5

For example, the Notices of the American Mathematical Society or the Gazette des mathématiciens.

6

Like the Leiden Declaration, this statement does not reject AI, a point lost on the authors of most of the negative comments on social media. The authors write

AI offers the potential of enhancing and accelerating genuine mathematical study and understanding. Mathematics as a profession will need to adapt to these changes in several ways. However, whether these changes ultimately benefit the field or have a destructive effect will in large part be determined by the decisions of the humans in control of this new technology.

7

Now more than 7700.

8

Admittedly, not all of these are professional mathematicians or mathematics students; but the vast majority do appear to be one or the other.

9

From a speech given in the U.S. Senate on April 21, 1830 by Rhode Island Senator Asher Robbins, and published in The Cherokee Phoenix, May 29, 1830. The Senator explains that the Cherokee see no resource or hope left to them because the United States has refused to honor its treaty guarantees.

In case you were wondering, I am not in the habit of reading the 19th century archives of the national newspaper of the Cherokee Nation. This reference was unearthed by Google’s AI-enhanced search function in response to a prompt whose phrasing I will leave to your imagination.

10

Added at noon on September 21: the Washington Post article’s place in the information landscape was illustrated today in a second Post article published today, with the title “Is this how the world ends?” The relevant passage:

Tegmark said that recent developments have made it easier to convince Americans that extinction risk from AI is real. Attempts to explain his views used to run aground in three places, he said. People doubted whether machines could really be smarter than humans and whether humans could really lose control of them, and struggled to grasp “why and how they would kill us all,” he said.

He considers the first two now widely understood, after AI models toppled a series of long-standing math problems and AI agents from OpenAI hacked into another company.

item.title: “If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice”
item.description: Fluid dynamics and an industrial midnight drama
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
My next post was supposed to be a celebration of proofsandprompts.com, a new forum where mathematicians can exchange ideas about the implications of generative AI for the future of the field, free from the noise and distortion created by the AI industry and its massive public relations apparatus. I was going to conclude by illustrating this noise and distortion with the genuinely awful Washington Post article about a one-day OpenAI “summit” to which a selected group of mathematicians were invited in early August. The article was awful not because of how it was written but because of what it reveals: that the AI industry is using prominent mathematicians as extras in a marketing operation masquerading as a drama, and that even the most sophisticated among the mathematicians play their roles, naively imagining that the drama is about them.

But just around midnight last night the drama turned significantly uglier, with more noise and distortion forecast over the next few days. Rumors have been circulating for just over a week that Anthropic was about to announce solutions to two of the Clay Millenium problems, specifically the Hodge Conjecture and the Navier-Stokes problem, though the details of the rumor fluctuated between proofs and counterexamples. I’ve written previously about AI and the Navier-Stokes problem and found that part of the rumor plausible; on the other hand, I know something about the Hodge Conjecture and saw absolutely no reason to believe that it was close to being solved, with or without LLMs. My intuition about the Hodge Conjecture rumor appears to have been correct. As for Navier-Stokes, the situation remains murky seven hours after Tristan Buckmaster made the following announcement on Mastodon:

Today, Levent Alpöge and I have made public three results: finite-time blowup with smooth forcing for incompressible porous media, for Boussinesq, and for 3d incompressible Euler.

The announcement was accompanied by links to three mathematical manuscripts and a statement by Buckmaster, which is where he talks about the Navier-Stokes problem. Over the last few minutes I have received four additional email messages, several of which refer to OpenAI’s behavior in this story as “research misconduct.” Read the following key paragraphs from Buckmaster’s statement and judge for yourselves.

Two proposals were offered to me. The first was that we post our Euler result, and that OpenAI post its Navier-Stokes result the next day. The second was that, after posting Euler, I alone write a paper presenting the Navier-Stokes result, acknowledging that an internal OpenAI model had resolved it. Sebastien twice asserted that he wanted Levent removed from authorship, and said it would all be simple if only it were not the case that, and it was so annoyingthat, Levent works at Anthropic. It was also said that if OpenAI posted after us, they would say that we deserved the Clay Prize, and that we were the “closest humans to the problem”. I declined both offers.

I said that if OpenAI released its result in the way proposed I would go public with what happened. The reply was, “Why would you ruin your career?” I replied that I am an academic, and asked why he thought going public would ruin my career. The reply was, “If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.”

Some time later Levent received a text proposing that he and Sebastien speak one on one, saying, “I don’t know if Tristan is being fully rational right now.”

Subscribe now

Some context is necessary. After announcing the results in the three manuscripts with Alpöge, Buckmaster continues:

We believe we also have blowup for hypo-dissipative Navier-Stokes. We are not releasing that paper today: unlike the above, the Lean verification has not yet finished. We do not yet have anything resembling a presentable writeup. I mention it because it is suggestive of a path to unforced Euler.

Buckmaster’s statement is four pages long. Page 1 is a description of the program that led to these results and the respective roles of the mathematicians and corporations involved; he writes specifically that “in view of this body of work, I believe Luis Martínez-Zoroa deserves a Fields Medal.” Pages 2 and 3 report on “another part of this story… that, honestly, I very much wish I did not have to be concerned with.” They describe a series of his email exchanges and conversations, starting September 3, centered on the claim that “an internal OpenAI model had produced a proof of finite time blowup for the forced Navier-Stokes equations.” The circumstances of this claim strongly suggest that OpenAI somehow got wind of what Buckmaster and Alpöge were doing and decided to scoop them.

You can call that what you like. Buckmaster is cautious, as well he should be when caught between corporations in a struggle to the death for market share, with trillions of dollars at stake and with access to literal armies of lawyers.

I would like to be clear about what I am not claiming. I have not seen OpenAI’s proof. I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used. I am not accusing anyone of anything. I am stating what I was told, when, and what was proposed to me. I am stating it because the alternative is to let a sequence of announcements say something I know to be false.

I believe the story speaks for itself, but I will leave the last word to Tony Vlasudich, who posted a comment on Mathstodon less than two hours after Buckmaster’s original message.

There would be little doubt in my mind that they would have access. These companies have zero scruples.

You may not wish to hear this, but it’s the price you will pay for selling your soul to the devil. The devil will keep you to the bargain.

Leave a comment

Readers are welcome to leave comments. I have other responsibilities over the next few days and will probably not be able to say more about this story. Meanwhile, I encourage you to let your imaginations run wild in speculating about just what the unnamed individual at OpenAI meant by “I don’t have to be nice.”

ADDED AFTER THE OpenAI ANNOUNCEMENT: According to the New York Times,

OpenAI said that it solved the Navier-Stokes problem using as many as 10,000 “A.I. agents” working in concert. Running such a large number of A.I. systems is likely to have cost millions of dollars, a result of the enormous amounts of electrical power needed to operate the specialized chips that drive A.I. technologies.

The Clay family created its million dollar prizes as a message that a great achievement in mathematics is deserving of a great reward. More precisely, to quote the Clay Mathematics Institute website:

The Prizes were conceived to record some of the most difficult problems with which mathematicians were grappling at the turn of the second millennium; to elevate in the consciousness of the general public the fact that in mathematics, the frontier is still open and abounds in important unsolved problems; to emphasize the importance of working towards a solution of the deepest, most difficult problems; and to recognize achievement in mathematics of historical magnitude.

Spending a multiple of the amount of the award1 in order to claim the achievement as part of a marketing operation, in contrast, is demeaning to mathematics, exploiting the dignity and prestige of the field in the most sordid and vulgar way imaginable.

This was sent to me on Wednesday morning:

1

“$22.5 million worth of compute, if charged at current Astra rates.” according to an article in TechCrunch entitled “OpenAI fought dirty on career-making math problem, says NYU mathematician.”

item.title: News, rumors, gossip
item.description: AI on everyone's mind
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
“How can I join the resistance?”

That, in effect, is the question I’ve been hearing at the conference I’m attending this week at the University of Utah, in honor of the 55th birthdays of number theorists Matt Emerton (University of Chicago) and Mark Kisin (Harvard). Graduate students and senior colleagues have come up to me to tell me they are regular readers of Silicon Reckoner; several have said explicitly that they agree with everything written here.

My purpose is not to boast. People are coming to me because for more than five years I have consistently been writing about mechanization of mathematics in a way that is not aligned with industry propaganda and the majority of media coverage but that apparently is consistent with how the majority of mathematicians, at least in my area, perceive developments in this area, and I have been the only mathematician doing so. I can’t claim that the positions expressed here are particularly original; regular readers will have seen numerous quotations from writers, business journalists, artists, and computer scientists, among others, who make arguments similar to mine, and who are almost all considerably better informed than I am. But it makes a difference to these colleagues and students that they are seeing these arguments being made by a mathematician. This is part of what it means to refer to mathematics as a community, and it’s something that the tech industry cannot replace.

The news is that I’m not, in fact, the only mathematician writing about mechanization and AI from a critical standpoint. I am aware of at least four new or recent developments:

  1. To start with the most immediately accessible: Max Weinreich, a specialist in algebraic dynamics who is moving to CUNY Baruch College in the fall, has “present[ed] the case for total opposition to the use of artificial intelligence in mathematics” in an arXiv preprint entitled “The crisis of AI-generated mathematics,” and will be giving a lecture on his proposal on September 11. Registration for the Zoom event is here.1

  2. Tasmin Chu, a graduate student in mathematics at Caltech, has just started a blog whose most recent entry, entitled, “The AI dissenter viewpoint” that asserts that “Mathematicians have moral obligations to resist AI companies” and calls for a “moratorium on asking LLMs to prove novel mathematical theorems.” Upon learning OpenAI’s announcement that its model had constructed a non-sofic group, Chu wrote a post concluding with the following prescriptions for mathematicians: Do not work for AI companies; Refuse all gifts and partnerships from AI companies; Use LLMs for mathematics judiciously, or desist from using them entirely. As of today (August 12) the blog has three lengthy posts on the implications and the social and political contexts of the development of AI for mathematics.

  3. This July Kirwin Hampshire, a PhD student at the University of Victoria, published a blog post entitled The Dark Night of Mathematics. This one, like Chu’s post, was also a reaction to recent events: an expression of a “profound spritual crisis due to” the construction by LLMs of “a number of counterexamples to significant long-standing conjectures.” In the space of just a few weeks, Hampshire’s essay has been “liked” nearly 1300 times and has generated more than 400 comments.

  4. And I have been contacted, undoubtedly not for the last time, by a colleague, whom I will not name for the moment, who is interested in developing a way to promote critical views within the profession.

It is not the case, notwithstanding the Monde Diplomatique headline, that “everyone hates AI” at this week’s conference. Some agree with Weinreich’s call for “total opposition” and some are ready for a “moratorium,” as in Chu’s post, while others, including all four of the colleagues with whom I had lunch on August 11, have one or more subscriptions to commercial AI services and use them, so far with moderation, in their mathematical research. But it is probably fair to say that, at the conference, “[almost] everyone hates” the AI industry, whether or not they have warm feelings for the technology. That aligns this branch of mathematics, at least, with the public opinion reflected in the Monde Diplomatique article that accompanies the headline.

                                          OpenAI open house for mathematicians

A frequent criticism of the Leiden Declaration is that it didn’t stress the potential benefits of AI for mathematics, as well as the threats. I find such a criticism frankly annoying, given that the news media have been bombarding us with claims about potential or even inevitable benefits for years, and the overwhelming majority of news coverage regarding AI and mathematics has been strictly aligned with industry messaging. Mathematicians quoted by the press may disagree with certain industry talking points, but most are on record sharing their belief that AI models will transform mathematics, and in a good way. This was also the message conveyed by nearly all AI-related activities at the ICM. It’s only recently — since the publication of the Leiden Declaration, to be more precise — that mathematicians who hold dissenting views have been given a public platform.

On the other hand, a rumor circulating at this week’s conference claims that a second Declaration is in the works, much more critical of AI than the Leiden Declaration. I had independently heard a similar rumor before leaving for the conference, and, rumors being what they are, I have no way to determine whether or not multiple Declarations may be made public in the coming months. It wouldn’t surprise me if the Monde Diplomatique diagnosis became the next big chapter in the continuing saga of AI disruption of mathematics.

One of the conference speakers confided to me that at least five of the young participants at this week’s conference believe that any colleague who opts to work with OpenAI or Anthropic or DeepMind or any of the other AI labs deserves to be shamed.2 I was not told their names and made no effort to identify them, but I assume the attitude is fairly widespread and growing.

Since I don’t know who among the 100 or so participants who are either students or early career researchers shares such attitudes, I can’t ask them how they feel about the “summit” held a few days ago at OpenAI, with the participation of a number of distinguished and more or less senior colleagues. I’ve been told that the meeting was “interesting” but the only concrete information I have about the event is that Daniel Litt gave a presentation, at the request of the organizers, and made his slides available on the internet, under the title “The End of Mathematics.” Litt writes,

The premise of the workshop (which we took as a starting point, rather than subject to debate, for the sake of productive discussion) was that AI will become robustly superhuman at mathematics. I want to tell a story in which, despite this, mathematical progress stalls. To be clear this is not a prediction--I'm optimistic by nature and think we'll find a way to adapt--but I am trying to imagine what a future in which certain existing trends continue might look like.

Fair enough. Litt’s slides do seem to have absorbed the dim view of human aspirations characteristic of Silicon Valley culture, as well as much of the local dialect — possibly the strongest argument in favor of shaming mathematicians tempted to defect, for the sake of their own ethical survival. But I don’t find his reasoning helpful in determining whether human mathematics will be going out with a bang or with a whimper; I suspect my reaction to any of the other presentations would be similar.

After reading Litt’s slides (or any other summit materials that may be made public), please ask yourself:

  • Does Litt’s “end of mathematics” scenario fill in the missing pages in the mathematical obsolescence script, by answering the questions at the end of this post?3

  • Does it answer the eight “questions to ask AI boosters” listed here?

  • Does it acknowledge the three kinds of “strongly negative” effects identified by Peter Scholze and quoted here: on “humanity, democracy and the planet”?

If you answer “no” to all three of the above questions, then you can safely ignore the scenario.

Subscribe now

                              Meanwhile, the new conquistadors take aim at math

And a few other quotations collected at random:

If you’re hearing somebody say AGI is imminent, and they’ve been saying it for years, and they seem to have a financial incentive for saying it . . . I think you should question why they’ve been wrong so far.

(Nick Frosst, quoted in Financial Times, June 19, 2025)

when I learned how the Saline data center saga played out, what happened was the Saline Township board, unlike a lot of boards, actually voted 4 to 1 against rezoning their land for the data center. So this was a case where local government said: This is not our vision for our community. It’s not worth it to us.

And what happened? The data center developers sued Saline Township, a town of, again, a few thousand people, saying: Wait, no, this is exclusionary zoning. You can’t have no industrial use in your entire township. And when a town of that size is getting sued by a giant A.I. data center developer, they just settled.

They were just like: Fine, give us a few million for the fire department and for some schools, and this fight is not worth it to us. But that, to people, felt like a profound violation of little-D democracy. …

And so I think that the data centers, in that sense, are a very visceral microcosm of the way that a lot of people feel that A.I. is showing up in their lives.

(Jasmine Sun with Ezra Klein, “The A.I. Giants weren’t prepared for this,” NY Times, August 4, 2026)

While Hassabis is widely admired for his scientific leadership, several people familiar with Google’s thinking said senior executives had become frustrated by what they saw as his lesser focus on the commercial demands of the company’s AI business.

His decision to make AlphaFold, the protein structure prediction system which earned him a Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024, freely available became a source of tension inside Google, according to a person familiar with the matter. The project generated little commercial return despite the scale of its investment. …

Alphabet’s shares fell 5 per cent following the announcements, underscoring concerns about the mounting cost of Google’s AI push and the pressure on the company to demonstrate it can translate its research strength into commercially successful products.

(Financial Times, August 8, 2026)

… unlike the robber barons of the past, who were often charitably minded and gave generously to public institutions, the tech billionaires of the present show a “complete indifference” to any kind of “social contract” and any need to “compensate people for the disruption they have brought into their lives”, says Quinn Slobodian, a historian of capitalism at Boston University.4

(Financial Times, August 9, 2026)

                                      Appendix:  a philosopher on Claude as author

Thanks to Justin Clarke-Doane for pointing me to an article entitled “Philosophy Journal Publishes Largely AI-Authored Article — On Purpose (guest post)” Simon Goldstein is the philosopher responsible for this news item. He writes

This month I published my first philosophy paper written with AI.

This may or may not be an accurate account of the situation, because the framing article makes the rather different claim, more consistent with the article’s title, that

Philosophy & Public Affairs recently—and knowingly—published an article written mostly by Claude, Anthropic’s LLM.

It may seem frivolous to worry whether the philosopher or the journal published the article (which I hope I don’t intend to read), but it’s only logical in view of Goldstein’s conclusion from this experiment that “the field will need to answer … how to credit Claude in papers like this one.” The framing article offers Goldstein the opportunity to explain the “Why and How” of his experiment. He writes

For this paper, I chose to credit Claude as a method for writing the paper: I included a lengthy acknowledgment about the use of Claude. An alternative approach would be to credit Claude as an author of the paper. I am also tempted by this approach.

One question is who exactly would be the author in the vicinity of Claude. I think of the name Claude as analogous to the term Homo sapiens: it describes a kind of agent rather than an agent. But the individual AI agents or instances that users work with are not usually given names. One convention going forward might be to assign a name of something like the form: “Claude Opus 4.7 time-stamp user-name”. That is probably enough information to uniquely identify the agent that assisted with the project.

So I am open to both attribution as a method and attribution as an author. But this is a broader question for the field to decide as the use of AI in writing philosophy becomes more common. Here we will need to reflect on the function of authorship. Among other things, authorship serves as a signal that readers can use to identify similar content, and as a tool for assigning responsibility. The question is whether assigning authorship to Claude improves these functions.

Some mathematicians, readers will recall, are also “tempted by” the notion of AI authorship. Goldstein goes on to make dramatic predictions regarding

The Future of Writing Philosophy

I suspect that in the next few years, AIs will be able to write philosophy papers without the help of a human PhD supervisor. At that point, human philosophy professors will have to find new tasks to perform. Maybe the whole job will be focused on undergraduate teaching, until AIs automate teaching. In the meantime, I hope to spend my time as a philosophy professor doing a mix of writing papers on my own and writing papers as a “PhD supervisor” for AIs.

Soon, AI will cause significant increases in the number of good philosophy papers submitted to journals. For the journal system to continue, journals must soon develop new AI-based refereeing tools, like Refine in economics, in order for journals to keep up. That said, once the number of good papers gets too large, the journal system as we know it will probably collapse.

Readers are left to imagine what happens to philosophy after the journal system’s collapse.

Leave a comment

1

Another Zoom event is scheduled in the same series, two weeks later, featuring mathematicians who are actively using and developing AI in mathematics. Half of the six listed panelists for this second event can be considered critical insofar as they have signed the Leiden Declaration.

2

Chapter 4 of my book Mathematics without Apologies, entitled “Megaloprepeia,” written more than 10 years ago, was intended in part to draw out the implications of training mathematicians to work for hedge funds. It could serve as a guide to shaming such people, but that’s not the sort of thing I could ever bring myself to do.

3

For the reader’s convenience I reproduce them here:

  • Where will that hypothetical superintelligent mathematics machine be built?

  • Who will operate it?

  • How will it be powered?

  • Who will build it?

  • And why?

4

See this post for a lengthy exposition of the tech billionaire transactional attitude to social contracts, specifically as regards higher education. Would your want your child to attend the College of Andreessen and Horowitz?

item.title: Quick clarification on authorship
item.description: Hoping to put this issue to rest for the moment
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
My most recent post makes the case that the Leiden Declaration’s position that “affirm[s] the humanity of authorship” is a political statement, and not a strict logical deduction from a hypothetic abstract universal concept of the author. This was meant to be a response to comments by several mathematicians who explained that they had not signed the Declaration because they believed that, under certain circumstances, authorship should be attributed to an AI system that has generated a valid proof. After I had finished the post, I learned that, on the very same day, OpenAI had issued a statement addressing this very point, in presenting its “Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science”:

The emergence of systems capable of contributing to mathematical research raises questions that cannot be answered by a technology company alone. There are many views as to the role of AI in mathematics, and we have deep respect and understanding for those concerned with its impact, including the signers of the Leiden declaration on AI and Mathematics. We believe attribution should honestly reflect how a result was produced: claiming human authorship for a proof generated entirely by an AI system would misrepresent both the system’s contribution and the nature of genuine human intellectual work. We helped prepare the manuscripts and formalize the proofs in Lean, and we take responsibility for their correctness, while the mathematical arguments themselves were generated by our system. We hope the mathematical community will engage deeply with these results, place them in context, and bring the ideas behind them to life through new research and discovery.

Subscribe now

I submitted the text to pangram.com to test for AI generation; the conclusion is that the red text was produced by AI, the rest by humans. Note how the AI-generated sentence1 directly contradicts the position on human authorship asserted unequivocally in the Leiden Declaration, which had been cited in the sentence immediately prior, which pangram identifies as human. Does this blatant contradiction reflect a conflict between OpenAI’s human managers and its LLM, that could someday spin out of control, with unpredictable consequences? Or is the “deep respect and understanding” claimed in the “human-generated” sentence just one more instance of OpenAI’s trademark insincerity, exemplified by founder Sam Altman, as memorably documented in Karen Hao’s Empire of AI and the New Yorker essay by Ronan Farrow and Andrew Marantz, in which Ilya Sutskever, apparently alluding to Altman, refers to the type of C.E.O. who “just tells people what they want to hear?”

OpenAI is apparently keen to have the material in this document attributed to its “next major model” Astra. In a private message, one of the Leiden Declaration’s authors observed

I find it sad but not at all surprising that OpenAI is trying to turn the issue of authorship on its head. It is very clever and extremely political of the OpenAI human team to say we take all responsibility and no credit…
