item.title: The Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics
item.description: Official press release, June 2, 2026
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
At 10 AM, June 2, 2026, Leiden University published a slightly adapted version of the press release copied below. At 12 noon Leiden time, all other outlets have been authorized to release the text.

The Leiden Declaration was developed by a group of participants in the workshop announced on this site in September 2025. I first announced the ongoing project to draft the Declaration last October 28. The process took a bit longer than anticipated, while different options for the scope of the planned Declaration were considered. These alternatives were discussed at length, by a group of authors whose relations to AI were extremely varied. The following Press Release describes the result. The Declaration itself can be read at its dedicated website.

AI is challenging the core values of mathematics: researchers call for urgent action

The rise of AI forces mathematicians to rethink what makes their field reliable and valuable. In the new ‘Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics’, an international group of researchers warns that AI is putting fundamental values of the discipline under threat.

What happens if a mathematical proof is no longer the work of a human, but of a proprietary AI model that academic researchers cannot access? Who is responsible for errors, and who gets credit if it is correct? And how can we tell whether an AI-generated proof is truly new, or simply a clever reformulation of existing work without proper attribution?

These are no longer hypothetical questions, but current dilemmas mathematicians worldwide are grappling with. That is why an international group of researchers from fifteen universities present the Leiden Declaration: a call to protect the core values of mathematics in the age of AI.

The declaration is endorsed by the International Mathematical Union (IMU). Ilka Agricola, chair of the IMU Committee on Publishing, explains: ‘AI is fundamentally transforming the way we do mathematics, and it is doing so at incredible speed. It offers fantastic possibilities when used honestly and competently as a “research assistant”. But this seems to be only a small part of what is going on: the by far larger part is a total mess where science itself is under attack.’

Among mathematicians, these developments have provoked a wide range of reactions. Peter Scholze, director of the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics and a 2018 recipient of the Fields Medal, the discipline’s highest honour, says: ‘This is a wonderful declaration, coming at the right time. The goal of mathematical research is human understanding of mathematics, and so mathematics can only thrive in a community of human mathematicians. It is crucial to preserve this communal spirit. In my experience, mathematical ideas, like children, must be nurtured and grow over the years. Just like I do not want my children to be educated by AI, I am pondering my mathematical ideas without use of AI, and generally avoid reading AI-generated text as best as I can.’

                                                       A call for action

The declaration does not ask for AI to be banned, but instead calls for action to ensure the continued flourishing of mathematics. AI is being used to write papers, generate proofs, and assist in peer review. According to the authors, the challenge is to ensure that the technology benefits rather than unrecoverably harms the discipline.

‘Recent AI-assisted results, such as the disproof of the unit distance conjecture by an internal OpenAI model, raise deep worries about closed access, inadequate attribution of related ideas, lack of transparency regarding methods and resource consumption, and much more’, says Rodrigo Ochigame of Leiden University, who co-organised the Lorentz Center workshop where the idea for a declaration emerged.

Five threats to mathematics

The declaration identifies five threats to the mathematical discipline.

1. A publication system overburdened with unreliable results

Mathematics is built on rigorous proofs that provide clear understanding. However, AI can produce ‘proofs’ that look convincing but contain almost invisible errors.

2. Lack of proper attribution and violation of copyright

AI models produce results without citing the human work they build on. This raises questions about recognition and intellectual property.

3. Dependence on AI for results to be considered significant

There is a risk that mathematicians will soon depend on access to the latest proprietary AI technology and expensive computational resources in order to produce competitive results. This leads to inequality between researchers.

4. Overhyping of results

Mathematics values work based on depth, difficulty, and significance. Press releases and blogs often make AI claims without scientific scrutiny. This leads to overestimation of AI capabilities and underestimation of human contributions.

5. Loss of autonomy

When technical feasibility or commercial interests shape research, mathematics risks losing autonomy in setting its research agenda.

On top of these, through AI many areas of mathematics suddenly get drawn into grave ethical concerns with regard to warfare, mass surveillance, political disruption, and environmental damage.

                                 What can individual mathematicians do?

‘AI has the potential to become a powerful partner in mathematical discovery. That power brings new responsibilities’, says Steven Strogatz, distinguished professor at Cornell University. ‘The Leiden Declaration calls on mathematicians to protect what makes our subject trustworthy and illuminating: proof, attribution, and the quest for insight.’

The declaration urges mathematicians to carefully disclose their use of AI and more generally live up to the spirit of open science. It advocates for affirming the humanity of authorship by taking responsibility of their work and putting effort into proper attribution. It encourages mathematicians to take their role in the public debate and to stay informed about the emerging technologies. They should carefully consider which tools to use, evaluate the ethical consequences of their activities and if necessary withdraw from harmful work.

‘The Leiden Declaration offers a helpful framework for mathematicians to decide how, when, and whether to engage with the new technologies.’

– Jeremy Avigad, professor at Carnegie Mellon University and central contributor to the Lean programming language and proof assistant

                                               What should organisations do?

The declaration urges research organisations and journals to take the lead in planning strategically and developing policy regarding the role of AI in mathematics. Leslie Ann Goldberg, head of computer science at the University of Oxford, underscores the urgency: ‘Inaccurate AI-generated drafts are cheap to produce, and there is a risk of cluttering the literature with claimed results that are simply wrong. Once that happens, the errors are likely to propagate as new results are built on faulty foundations.’

For maintaining standards of rigour, protecting the rights of authors, and guaranteeing proper forms of research output, collective action is necessary. Organisations should counterbalance the asymmetric bargaining position of individual researchers entering collaborations with industry by providing access to legal representation and by facilitating the development of codes of professional practice. Finally, funding agencies should take the values of the declaration into account in their evaluation procedures.

Professional societies can play a vital role. According to Agricola, ‘The IMU Committee on Publishing is deeply worried by the current situation, and hence we strongly welcome and support the community effort that led to the Leiden Declaration. Mathematics as we know and love it is at stake!’

                                          What is needed from governments?

According to the declaration, governments should regulate the AI industry and invest in public alternatives to commercial technologies, so that power is not concentrated in private hands.

                                             Requests to commercial AI

The declaration requests collaborations with industry to abide by the same standards expected of academic research. Kevin Buzzard, a professor at Imperial College London who has become a leading figure in the computer formalisation of mathematics, writes: ‘Mathematicians should find it quite striking that tech companies are suddenly interested in their work. The Leiden Declaration is a well-thought-through response to what is currently happening, as AI continues to disrupt this space.’

                                                        Beyond mathematics

Although the declaration focuses on mathematics, the authors stress that similar issues arise in other academic fields and creative industries. The discussion therefore raises a broader question: how do we maintain control, reliability, and recognition in a rapidly changing technological landscape?

The message of the Leiden Declaration is clear: AI offers major opportunities, but without clear choices and shared responsibility, it places the foundations of science under severe pressure. According to the authors, we need to act now.

From workshop to declaration

The idea for a declaration emerged during the NIAS-Lorentz Workshop on Mechanization and Mathematical Research in September 2025, which discussed the implications of rapid developments in technology for the practice of mathematics. The event brought together around sixty researchers from ten countries – including mathematicians, computer scientists, and scholars from the humanities and social sciences – and also included a public symposium.

The Leiden Declaration was written by a working group of sixteen participants from this larger group, convened by Jim Portegies of the Eindhoven University of Technology and in consultation with a wide range of members of the mathematical community.

The authors are Jarod Alper (University of Washington), Michael Barany (University of Edinburgh), Alain Chavarri Villarello (Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam), Sander Dahmen (Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam), Walter Dean (University of Warwick), Karthik Ganapathy (University of California, San Diego), Michael Harris (Columbia University), David Holmes (Leiden University), Mateja Jamnik (University of Cambridge), Steven Kelk (Maastricht University), Bryna Kra (Northwestern University), Ursula Martin (University of Oxford), Bartosz Naskręcki (Adam Mickiewicz University and Warsaw University of Technology), Rodrigo Ochigame (Leiden University), Jim Portegies (Eindhoven University of Technology), and Johannes Schmitt (ETH Zurich).

The original version of this article was published by Leiden University.

Note added shortly after noon June 2:

The New York Times and Scientific American have now both posted articles reporting on the Leiden Declaration.

item.title: About that Erdős problem
item.description: Another missed opportunity for mathematicians
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
Although I was busy with the kind of activity that typically occupies the time and the imagination of a working mathematician, and that we have every reason to believe will continue to do so for the foreseeable future, though it doesn’t attract much attention from the news media, it was impossible to avoid hearing about OpenAI’s latest announcement concerning the construction (in less than five pages) of a counterexample to the Erdős unit distance conjecture.

The announcement contained comments by nine prominent mathematicians. It came in the middle of a week marked by more than the usual crop of news items about AI. OpenAI was notably gearing up for an IPO, as was Anthropic, while SpaceX’s filing with Nasdaq included language like

the light of consciousness will not be tied to a single planet subject to the inevitable hazards of a harsh and vast universe

Those of us whose pensions depend on financial markets are thus on track to share in the losses as well as profits from Silicon Valley’s massive bets, because, as Financial Times reports

…new “fast entry” rules thrust the stocks straight into Wall Street indices.

The rules, implemented this month by Nasdaq, mean billions of dollars of passive money will automatically flow to the three companies shortly after they go public, driving their share prices higher but forcing investors to sell other stocks

It was also the week when Eric Schmidt, former Google CEO, was one of several speakers met with boos at college commencements, and articles about the AI backlash filled both major and obscure media,1 so that Obama’s campaign manager David Plouffe is warning of a “political backlash that could make AI the dominant issue in the 2028 presidential race.”

Finally, this was the week when Trump, reacting to “pressure from Silicon Valley,”

scrapped the signing of an executive order that was expected to lay out partnerships with leading AI companies to vet cutting-edge models

thus postponing meaningful regulation yet again.

So how did those nine mathematicians take advantage of this exceptional opportunity to participate in, or at least to show they are not totally oblivious to, what may well be the most consequential political issue of our time, one of the few that genuinely appears to transcend partisan divisions?

Subscribe now

The end of Victor Wang’s contribution came closest to meeting the challenge of the moment:

The implicit social contract between mathematicians and AI companies deserves further attention. When Hajir, Maire, and Ramakrishna wrote their beautiful papers [19, 20], did they have in mind that an AI might eventually use their work (as the CoT likely indicates) to derive headline results, potentially with significant ensuing financial implications? When we make our work freely available on the arXiv, do we all implicitly want it to be freely available to AI as well?

I do not want to comment further on the trajectory of AI, which seems to me to be a complicated question involving physics, materials, society, and the environment.

Melanie Matchett Wood’s comment pointed out reasons to be cautious about drawing conclusions from the OpenAI announcement —

This result does not show us all the times AI has claimed to have a proof of something and been wrong. Without that context (which many of us have just from personal experience), it is also easy to draw incorrect conclusions about the current state of AI and research mathematics.

but did not address the concerns behind the growing AI backlash. And Tim Gowers included a parenthentical remark, in the middle of his characteristically thoughtful analysis of technical matters related to the finding of a counterexample:

(Here I am assuming that there will at least be the usual kinds of efficiency gains, where what a large model can do this year, a much smaller one can do next year. Without that, solving lots of problems might be too expensive, not to mention environmentally unfriendly.)

That’s all. But there will undoubtedly be opportunities in the future, as the Wall Street Journal is simultaneously running articles about OpenAI’s upcoming IPO and warnings by engineers that “The artificial intelligence supposedly capable of replacing well-paid software developers is flooding the world with bad, potentially even dangerous, code.” Let’s hope our colleagues will not be afraid to participate in the public debate.

If I were asked what I think of the OpenAI announcement, I would quote Cal Newport’s observation in Gary Marcus’s Substack newsletter, which is consistent with the questions raised in my previous post:

There are few markets smaller and less lucrative than professional academic mathematics.

And then I would defer to the quotation from environmental policy analyst Amanda Ianthe Greene, which you can read on Graham Lovelace’s Substack newsletter, under the headline “The backlash against AI is real, and growing. How might Big Tech respond?”:

“No, Eric Schmidt, the question is not ‘whether we will shape AI’,” Ianthe Greene wrote:

“The question is who owns it, who controls how it’s used, who benefits from it, who profits from it. AI was built on the backs of all of us. Our writing, our art, our social media, our personal data, our research and reports. We should all own it and share in the profits.”

Leave a comment

1

A few headlines: The AI backlash is the only thing growing faster than AI revenues; Has the great AI backlash begun?, AI CEOs Baffled by Hatred of Their Technology, Growing AI backlash in the US sparks public protests, election debates.

item.title: Questions to ask AI boosters
item.description: To print on a stack of flash cards and keep in reserve
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
AI companies and their models will follow one rule before all others: they will seek to maximise returns for their shareholders, up to the limits set by law. When the law of profit conflicts with the company’s internal principles, profit will win every time.1

                                   8 questions, preceded by one anti-question

Chances are you have the opportunity, every week if you so choose, to attend a meeting2 or a seminar or a public lecture where the speakers try to convince you that the arrival of AI in your neighborhood or your workplace or your discipline is both inevitable and ultimately beneficial, or else that it represents a transformation of the conditions of life on a scale much greater than that of the industrial revolution, or all of the above.

The questions listed below are guaranteed to enliven any such presentation. The list was not hard to compile; every day the press publishes new articles about the AI backlash.3 I just collected a few of the main conclusions and turned them into questions. It took me less than 10 minutes. ChatGPT couldn’t have done better!

  1. First, avoid questioning claims about AI capabilities unless you are an expert. You don’t want to get confounded by a technical question you can’t answer. For the same reason, talking about apocalyptic scenarios is a pointless distraction.

  2. AI systems don’t build themselves. So the first and most important question is (in several parts): who will build the system? Who will pay for it? How will the decisions to provide the necessary infrastructure be made? What happens if the public refuses?

  3. What will be the cost in resources? What other needs will go unfulfilled when these resources are diverted to AI?

  4. What will be the environmental cost? What communities will bear these costs, locally and internationally?

  5. The investment in the technology is at an unprecedented scale, and it is a bet on future returns. What happens if the bet is unsuccessful? Are these corporations too big to fail, and will the public be on the hook, with the prospect of long-term austerity, as in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis? How can the public be protected from such an outcome?

  6. It is frequently claimed that the dot-com bubble, like the raiload bubble more than a century earlier, actually provided valuable long-term investment, in the form of the infrastructure for the subsequent spectacular growth of the internet. This is advanced as an argument that even if the current excessive dependence of the economy on the tech sector is a speculative bubble, the infrastructure left behind will power future growth. But others claim that the technology is evolving so rapidly that data centers built today will be obsolete by the time the economy recovers from the bursting of the bubble. Is this a valid argument?

  7. Along the same lines, mainstream and heterodox economists have been arguing over the likely implications downstream of massive implementation of AI in the labor process. Daron Acemoglu claims that AI has not in fact increased productivity. This article in Jacobin invokes orthodox economic arguments to speculate that AI implementation will lead to stagnation.4 Won’t this discourage investment?

  8. The tech industry is massively spending to prevent the election of candidates favorable to regulation of AI. Doesn’t the concentration of economic power in the industry distort the political process?

  9. More generally, haven’t we already seen how the unprecedented concentration of wealth and power in the industry is a danger to democracy, especially since the leaders have repeatedly shown themselves to be hostile to democratic decisions?

                                                                           Tips

Tech is often spoken of in an airy and disembodied language—“genies” and “clouds.” This hides the fact that it is as physical and real as coal and worms.

(Molly Crabapple, Critical AI, April 2026)

  1. Don’t worry that the questions will be irrelevant to the presentation. All these presentations say essentially the same thing.

  2. Don’t worry that the talk will already have included convincing answers to these questions. It would be a miracle if it does, and miracles sometimes happen. But it’s unlikely.

  3. It’s more fun to share the questions with friends. Hand out flash cards and sit in different parts of the auditorium.

  4. If you can’t convince your friends to come along, don’t make the mistake of trying to ask all the questions. You’ll just come across as a nutcase if you do. I know this from personal experience.

  5. The Simons Foundation has just announced that

    AI Will Be Top of Mind at ICM, Math’s Biggest Conference

    So those of you who plan to attend the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia (if you have not chosen to boycott the Congress) will have the opportunity to test these questions (and don’t forget to sample the local scrapple!) no later than this coming July. I’ll probably be at the ICM, but only for a day.

(I wasn’t familiar with the expression “top of mind” and wondered whether it wasn’t a misprint, or an invention of an LLM. But in fact it has been a part of the English language since around 1980, according to Google n-grams, started to take off in 2000, and has been growing rapidly since 2014. Its chief use appears to be in the expression “top-of-mind awareness,” which Wikipedia informs us

is a measure of how aware is a consumer of a brand. It is part of consumer behaviour, and is a key aspect of marketing research and marketing communications.

Exactly where Math’s Biggest Conference will want to keep AI.)

Subscribe now

                                     One more question for mathematicians

The Simons Foundation news page cited above refers to Rutgers number theorist Alex Kontorovich as an “evangelist”: “The sooner AI and humans formalize known math, Kontorovich says, the sooner a broader set of researchers can use AI to assist with mathematical discovery.”

But though he may be an evangelist, Kontorovich is not naive about industry intentions.

So let’s separate what how decisions are made collectively from what profit seeking corporations like Math Inc, Axiom, and Amazon and so on are doing in mathematics. You might say they should get out of mathematics. They shouldn’t be involved in this subject at all. I actually think in five years they will be out of mathematics because they’re only using mathematics right now to prove who’s the best among them. Math is a really really easy playground and the only reason they’re involved is because that’s a playground where by doing some publicity stunt they get to attract VC funding. Okay? And then they’ll get bored of us and they’ll move on and we’ll be back to just doing math for our own sake. In the process though they might develop all kinds of amazing tools that help us learn new mathematics. And so that’s my viewpoint in working with them.

(Alex Kontorovich, edited YouTube transcription)

The “you” on the second line may have been addressed to me personally, since he was responding to my question. In fact I was not arguing that the corporations shouldn’t be involved in mathematics, but rather that soon they wouldn’t any longer be interested in mathematics; in other words, just what Alex confirmed was his own expectation.

There was no time for the follow-up question, but maybe one of you can ask it if you attend Alex Kontorovich’s plenary talk at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia this coming July:

9. If these powerful corporations have promised their investors that they will soon “solve” mathematics, how will they react if they see human mathematicians “doing math for our own sake”? At the very least, wouldn’t they be concerned about the insufficient “top-of-mind awareness” of their brand, and wouldn’t they be motivated to do something about it?

And, more prosaically, wouldn’t claims on the part of the industry to have “solved” mathematics be in tension with claims on the part of mathematicians to need public funding in order to continue “doing math for our own sake”?

Leave a comment

1

Robert Armstrong, “AI companies are just companies,” Financial Times, April 30, 2026. Armstrong is FT’s US financial commentator; he originated the expression “TACO trade.”

2

I missed this big one, sponsored in part by something called the Futures of Mathematics Institute, which, tellingly, is not run by mathematicians (note the plural).

3

Some recent (and not so recent) headlines:

The AI Backlash Is Here: Why Public Patience With Tech Giants Is Running Out

(Jesus Mesa, Newsweek, October 3, 2025)

The AI Backlash Could Get Very Ugly

(Lila Shroff, The Atlantic, May 13, 2026)

The AI Industry Is Discovering That the Public Hates It

(Luke Barnes, The New Republic, April 24, 2026)

A.I. Populism Is Here. And No One Is Ready.

(David Wallace-Wells, New York Times, May 8, 2026)

item.title: Who speaks for mathematics?
item.description: Can we help journalists choose?
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
A handful of journalists around the world are responsible for extracting publishable copy from the blizzard of press releases about the latest Milestones™ achieved in the machine’s struggle to outstrip the “intellectual power and speed”1 of human mathematicians. Since it obviously wouldn’t do just to reproduce the press releases verbatim, and since journalists are not so suicidal as to hand over their assignments voluntarily to Claude or ChatGPT, they have to find material to place the new developments in context. The role of a science journalist, however, is not to tell the reader what to think, but rather to find a recognized authority figure who will tell the reader what to think. To help the reader recognize the legitimate authority of their chosen interlocutor, the journalist can point to various external markers, and the Fields Medal is a popular choice. But you have to find a Fields Medalist interested in speaking to the press. This is how Terence Tao “has become a prominent scorekeeper for AI’s push into” mathematics, to quote a recent article in Scientific American.

It’s probably largely in connection with AI that Tao is actually on the verge of becoming something of a household name, so that I have heard his name come up on four completely unrelated occasions in the last two weeks: at a roundtable discussion at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, in two separate conversations I had at the American Philosophical Society in Philadelphia, and in a telephone call with a concierge in Paris. On each of these occasions Tao was cited as the source for a prophecy about AI and mathematics, where mathematics was not the main topic but rather a proxy for human capabilities as such.

Subscribe now

Over the past few years Peter Scholze has been cited about half as frequently, according to Google n-grams

and rarely in connection with AI. So I was grateful when he wrote the other day to tell me that he had been quoted as part of a German initiative, under the umbrella of the international campaign PauseAI, to call upon the German delegation to the AI Impact summit in Delhi to speak out for a global agreement based on two priorities:

  1. Clear limits on the use of AI to avoid unacceptable global consequences, and

  2. Binding safety standards, regulated by an independent international enforcement body.

The call was signed by 140 German scientists, and included quotations from 22 of them, including the one reproduced above, and which I translate:

I already consider the influence of AI to be strongly negative, for humanity, for democracy, and for the planet.2

(I note in passing that “bereits jetzt” is one of those expressions that doesn’t have a perfect equivalent in English, one more argument against eliminating incentives to learn foreign languages.)

Scholze’s statement, according to this report, was taken from a press release3, which I assume also included a quotation by Heidelberg mathematician Otmar Venjakob; the latter’s quotation is also reproduced on the website of the German call:

Als Dekan für Mathematik und Informatik habe ich die Begeisterung über KI-Fortschritte jeden Tag erlebt. Nicht zuletzt durch die intensive Auseinandersetzung im Rahmen unserer Vortragsreihe 'KI und Ethik' habe ich aber auch eine Vielzahl offener Sicherheitsbedenken und ethischer Fragestellungen erkannt, die mit jedem Fähigkeitssprung drängender werden. Ein internationaler Ordnungsrahmen ist daher längst überfällig.

The last sentence says that an international framework for AI is long overdue; I’ll leave it to readers to choose whether or not to translate the rest.

So there are two voices for mathematics that readers have probably not heard, unless they are in Germany. I’ll return to this question in a future post, with a modest proposal for creating once and for all a single authoritative voice to speak for mathematics.

Leave a comment

1

A quotation from the article Heuristic Problem Solving: The Next Advance in Operations Research by Herbert Simon and Alan Newell, Operations Research, Vol. 6, No. 1 (Jan. - Feb., 1958), pp. 1-10.

2

I am fully in agreement with this statement, provided however that by AI we understand the military contractors and startups that currently dominate the sector. My feelings about the technology as such are less categorical, provided it can be separated from the commercial interests.

3

Originally mistranslated as “press conference,” now corrected.

item.title: Quanta smashes the Overton window
item.description: Mathematicians are informed: this is the future
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
And the angel of history cried, “This can’t be happening!”

With their characteristic subtlety, Quanta took a sledgehammer to the Overton window on AI and mathematics and let in the hurricane. “Mathematicians think this is just the beginning,” announces the subtitle to the article whose title you can read on the banner above. In this way Quanta’s editors are sending a message to future historians: mathematicians in 2026 are the ones who do battle under the banner reading “The AI Revolution [not an AI Revolution] Has Arrived;” the rest merit at most a footnote.

Readers of Silicon Reckoner will recognize this as a return to form on Quanta’s part. Just last month Leila Sloman published a careful and thoughtful article on formalization. Sloman went to the trouble of speaking to mathematicians with a variety of views on the significance of the current trends in formalization, rather than assembling quotes from those conforming to a predetermined line. More surprisingly, her editor let her publish what she discovered:

As with past attempts to formalize math, Lean has generated mixed feelings. Some mathematicians look forward to offloading tedious verification work onto computers and see Lean as a potentially transformative new way of doing mathematics. Others think that their time and resources are better spent elsewhere — or, worse, that a Lean-centric approach will distort the true value of mathematics. It’s a discussion that’s starting to play out in the hallways of math departments around the world: How do we balance the creativity needed to discover new mathematical connections with the rigor needed to ensure that every logical step is undeniable?

Subscribe now

You’ll find nothing like this in today’s article, over the byline of Konstantin Kakaes. Practically everyone who was quoted is marching under the same banner. There are expressions of concern:

In asking what AI is doing to mathematical research, we shouldn’t only look at the successes. Litt cautioned that “there is a lot of pollution of the commons by AI-generated nonsense.” Joel David Hamkins (opens a new tab) of the University of Notre Dame said he is “despairing of this ocean of slop that is overwhelming our journal systems.”

but this despair can be cured:

Mathematicians are pinning their hopes on formal proof as the way to navigate this ocean of slop. They’re converting proofs into a language that computers can understand, and then using computer programs to verify that all the logic in the proof pans out.

The link you see in that last excerpt is a Sloman’s March article, of which it represents a blatant misreading, unless you agree to redefine “mathematicians” as suggested above.

Maybe I’m reading too much into Kakaes’s failure (or his editor’s failure) to refer to Sloman’s article except through that link, in contrast to the presence of a link to the 2025 article that was the subject of this post under the heading “RELATED” at the bottom of Kakaes’s article.

Last night I wondered whether I should really have been staying up past midnight to finish a post about how impossible it is to keep up with all the news stories about AI and mathematics. The subtext, which I should have taken greater care to spell out, is that, unless you do put in the time, your beliefs regarding what I called “the unfolding inter-species love story between human and AI mathematics” will inevitably be shaped — and distorted — by those forces with the most extensive resources for promoting their perspective. In that sense, last night’s post can be read as a warning about this morning’s Quanta story. Although I know at least half of the people interviewed for that story, I had no idea it was about to be published when I finished last night’s post. And yet in another sense I did!

Leave a comment

item.title: Notes from the front
item.description: A sampling of the latest news; or, how not to drown in the same river twice
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
Anyone who hopes to write a serious scholarly report on the latest developments in the unfolding inter-species love story between human and AI mathematics has to accept that the time lag between submitting a final draft and publication is so long that any published account you read will be hopelessly out of date. Unless, of course, it is written in the style of a journalistic scoop; then it will be maybe no more than a few hours out of date, but it will be hopelessly superficial — more or less shallow depending on your editor’s mood.

                                       Did we sleep through the Singularity?

When I woke up this morning I fully intended to report on two papers posted in March and February1 — an unconscionably long time ago — that were “generated autonomously” by the AI model Aletheia, developed by Berkeley mathematician (and my occasional co-author) Tony Feng. Here is Feng’s explanation:

The mathematical content of this paper was entirely generated, end-to-end, by an internal reasoning agent built upon Gemini Deep Think, codenamed Aletheia at Google DeepMind [aletheia]. The paper itself was rewritten by the human author, starting from Aletheia’s output. However, by comparing the paper to the model outputs linked above, the reader can verify that Aletheia’s original output is already complete and correct in mathematical content. Thus the author’s only contribution to this paper (aside from developing Aletheia) was to fiddle with the exposition, and to write an Introduction.

The results are mathematically significant and definitely demonstrate something, but it’s not clear what. The first obvious question is: how was Aletheia trained? Was it trained on the Collected Works of Everybody (humans and human-Neanderthal hybrids alike), as I suspect Gemini Deep Think was, in which case it would be one stage in the greatest math heist in history, and a prelude to enclosure of the commons? For readers of this newsletter that doesn’t count as news. A more subtle question concerns the subsequent steps of training. What kinds of problems was Aletheia trained to solve? The article introducing Aletheia lists more authors than I care to count. How many hours of human labor went into training? The first six pages of the paper include hints of what makes Aletheia different from previous systems. In a section entitled “Importance of tool use,” for example, we read

In contrast to the structured, bounded nature of IMO problems, mathematical research requires synthesizing published literature to address broader, open-ended questions. We observed that simply granting internet access is insufficient; however, when our model was extensively trained for tool use, the integration of Google Search and web browsing led to a substantial reduction in obvious citation hallucinations with fictitious titles and/or authors. This shifted citation errors to subtler hallucinations, for example where the reference exists but its results are not quoted properly.

The really enlightening answers, however, are missing, and, I suppose, are protected by industrial secrecy and non-disclosure agreements.

Is Aletheia meant to be a prototype of a future problem-solving and theorem-proving system that will serve as the mathematician’s “junior co-author,” as in a widely misquoted interview with Terence Tao? Or is it DeepMind’s latest shiny bait to attract private equity investors and venture capital that would otherwise be funding the competition? The website of the Milestones of Autonomous Mathematics workshop, sponsored by ICARM and Principia Labs, which is taking place this week in San Francisco, asks the same question in the form of a declarative sentence:

In absence of proper incentives, AI companies rush towards low-hanging fruit that generate good headlines with little serious vision or long-term strategy for deep autonomous research.

I would love to spend time sharing my thoughts on the impact Aletheia’s apparent solution of 6 of the First Proof problems may or may not have on DeepMind’s global image, but that was yesterday’s news; today I have to report, superficially, on the Milestones workshop, before that memory too fades into oblivion.

Subscribe now

                            Collaborating in the enclosure of the commons

Now is the time for mathematicians to come together and define for the world what are the potential developments in AI that would be exciting, useful, and valuable to the community. What are the facets of an autonomous math researcher or assistant, and is it possible to measure progress in the relevant capabilities?

Any answer to these questions must emphasize the diversity and multidimensionality of mathematics. This workshop is intended to produce a list of milestones marking levels of progress in each of roughly 8 categories of assistance or reasoning a math AI may provide researchers. These categories or “skillsets” will be determined on the first day, by a consensus of the participants on what would be most valuable to the community, but will likely be broad and fundamental abilities such as “Problem solving,” “Generalization,” “Exposition,” “Formalization,” and “Conjecturing.”

(from the Milestones workshop announcement)

I was invited to fly out to San Francisco (at my own expense) to be put up (not at my expense) near Principia’s headquarters, by the 16th St. Mission BART station, to help “define for the world” the kind of AI that mathematicians would find “exciting, useful, and valuable.” Responsibilities in New York made that impossible, but after my Thursday morning class I Google-met with workshop participants for an hour or so, to catch up on the week’s activities. I will have to spend many hours reading the documents that the Milestones workshop is producing in the — apparently sincere — hope of providing the “proper incentives” and the “serious vision or long-term strategy for deep autonomous research” that is missing from the corporate agenda.

In the online chat I couldn’t resist carping about the incongruity of the vastness of the ambition of the week-long program together with its flagrant disregard for historical perspective:

Clearly the authors of the collected drafts have devoted serious thought to articulating their theoretical beliefs about the concrete values underlying mathematical practice as experienced today. I would have liked to see an acknowledgment that this formulation needs to be judged in the light of thousands of years of writing about the very same topics in hundreds of significant documents, but today’s mathematicians have the habit, which is often productive, of believing that it is their responsibility to keep reinventing the wheel.

If the pill has been invented that will make my writing more mellow,2 I haven’t seen it. But I hope to address the Milestones documents’ failure to refer to the collected wisdom of human mathematicians reflections upon our vocation after I have had the time to read them (next week, by which time they will be so far out of date that no one will care what I think); because in the minutes that remain before midnight I want to explain what the whole process brings to mind.

Formerly, the peasant family produced the means of subsistence and the raw materials, which they themselves, for the most part, consumed. These raw materials and means of subsistence have now become commodities…. Yarn, linen, coarse woollen stuffs — things whose raw materials had been within the reach of every peasant family, had been spun and woven by it for its own use — were now transformed into articles of manufacture, whose markets were none other than the country districts.3 …Thus, hand in hand with the expropriation of the self-supporting peasants, with their separation from their means of production, goes the destruction of rural domestic industry, the process of separation between manufacture and agriculture. (Marx, Capital, Volume I, Chapter 30)

Substitute mathematics departments for Marx’s peasant families and we see where the corporate appropriation of our profession’s raw materials, exemplified by DeepMind’s Aletheia and abetted by the Milestones process, leads: the means of mathematical subsistence will wind up enclosed behind the electrified fences of proprietary algorithms. Having donated to the industry hours of sincere effort to draft comprehensive clarifications of what we genuinely value in our vocation, those of us who remain stuck in our country districts have to buy back mathematics in the form of articles of manufacture, such as the 10000 page proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, humanly incomprehensible but formalized and verified, that popped up, right on schedule, in a 15-minute exchange during the online Milestones discussion, as it inevitably comes up whenever the conversation turns to the long-term implications of AI for mathematics.

The problem with this picture, as I’ve already explained more than once, is that there is no viable market for manufactured mathematics, at least not for the theoretical kind that occupied the minds of my colleagues.4 Alex Kontorovich, one of the organizers of the Milestones workshop, explicitly acknowledged this when he spoke at Columbia last week at an event on formalization and autoformalization. I don’t want to misquote him, but I’m pretty sure he said that he expected an inter-species break up, between AI and human mathematicians, within the next 5 years; however, in the meantime he hoped, as others in San Francisco seem to hope, that something good will come of it for mathematicians. Which means, I suppose, something that is more than our own labor being sold back to us.

I want to finish up before midnight, which is only 5 minutes away, but before I leave I want to draw readers’ attention to a different approach to AI evaluation, announced today by Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan, authors of the book AI Snake Oil and of the blog AI as Normal Technology. How does the following compare with what the mathematicians are doing this week in San Francisco?

AI models have started to saturate most major benchmarks. But does that mean they can build and ship a real product, or conduct a scientific experiment end-to-end, or navigate a government bureaucracy? Researchers have started testing AI in such real-world settings. We call these evals “open-world evaluations”. This essay defines open-world evaluations, surveys the lessons learned so far, and lays out best practices for conducting them.

The answer will have to wait until the next post, by which time the question will already be out of date.

Added after midnight

I forgot to include this comment that I had also posted in the online chat during the Milestones meeting:

I usually don’t like to make predictions, but I’m fairly confident of my prediction of how the Milestones documents will affect mathematics in the long run. The industry will cite them as an expression of the values of MATHEMATICS and of thoughtful leading mathematicians, and will then direct their efforts to reaching these milestones, in order to make an impression on their investors and the media. When this round is over, they will no longer have any need for mathematics (within 5 years, according to several people who were participating in this morning’s conversation). Prime Minister Farage will then quote industry figures as justification for severe reduction of research funding for human mathematics.

Leave a comment

1

Eigenweights for arithmetic Hirzebruch proportionality, by Tony Feng, and The simplicity of the Hodge bundle, by Anand Patel. In the interest of full disclosure: as soon as Feng’s article was posted on the arXiv, I solicited it as editor of Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences NEXUS, where it has been accepted for publication.

2

This word was used literally in every other sentence when I first visited San Francisco.

3

I modified the standard translation of this passage to clarify the point.

4

RELX, the company formerly known Reed Elsevier, does indeed have a market capitalization of $64.56 billion, making it the world's 376th most valuable company. Elsevier does indeed have a market in university libraries and, like the manufacturers of woollen goods in Marx’s history, they do make a profit selling our work back to us. As the statement I signed in 2012 asks, “Why do mathematicians contribute all this volunteer labor, and their employers pay all this money, for a service whose value no longer justifies its cost?” But the market for mathematics represents a negligible proportion of that market capitalization.

item.title: Don't "like" this essay!
item.description: Thoughts inspired by Antonio Casilli's Waiting for Robots
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
A “like” on Facebook is estimated at between $0.0005 (a value calculated by a downward auction mechanism between a social platform and an ad sales platforms), $0.004 (if you buy 1100 likes for less than $5 on a click farm platform), and $174 (according to a marketing agency’s estimate of the purchase cost for a potential customer).

(Antonio Casilli, Waiting for Robots)

Today we celebrate all those readers who keep social media at arm’s length by refraining from sinking into the behavioral ruts into which social media attempts to steer us, thus escaping involuntary and possibly irreversible devolution into human bandwidth. No ❤️s, ❤️‍🔥s, 😂s, emerge from their keystrokes; no ratings on Yelp or Google or Goodreads or (especially) Amazon; and no obsessive markings with thumbs-up or thumbs-down or thumbs-sideways on news media comment sections.

Readers who approve of today’s essay and feel compelled to register their approval are invited to celebrate by steering clear of the little heart at its top left, under my picture, and writing something in the comments section (and not “like”-ing anyone else’s comments, either); readers who approve but wish to keep their approval to themselves can celebrate by doing just that; and readers who disapprove are invited to celebrate by sharing their reasons for disapproval, again in the comments. And I will celebrate by doing what I always do, or rather not doing what I never do, which is clicking on the “like” button.

It’s not that I don’t hunger for positive reinforcement. On the contrary, I’m feel a twinge of gratitude every time Substack checks in with the news that I have a new subscriber (now up to 1601!) or a new follower (2567 as of today) and certainly on those infrequent occasions when someone, who is almost always unknown to me,

liked If mathematics is an art form, why don’t we think like artists?

or some other essay.

Nor is it because the “like” button — “the button that changed the world,” according to the subtitle of the book by Martin Reeves and Bob Goodson whose title is simply LIKE — is, as a reviewer of this book claims, “the nicotine in the cigarette of our online lives,” which brought about a world of “people going online precisely in order to like and be liked.”

We have gone [says the reviewer] in quick succession from the kneejerk responses of trolling and outrage on social media to the lazy gallery of emoticons and cartoon emojis, to the climax of a reaction so undemanding as to make it almost empty of meaning — the like.

As art critic Jonathan Crary put it,

How does one remain human in the bleakness of this world when the ties that connect us have been shattered and when malevolent forms of rationality are powerfully at work?1

Kneejerk responses and the “like” button contribute to shattering the “ties that connect us” and replace them with algorithmic rationality, but that comment on how the internet debased and debases human relations can be kept in reserve for a future occasion.

Nor, finally, is it that I feel guilty for reaping the “like”s of others while sowing none of my own, so that, not only do I stand out as a reprobate for my lack of emotional generosity; my failure to meet my quota means that some other unfortunate will have to work overtime to maintain the average of “every person on the planet liking something 20 times a day,” to quote the reviewer of LIKE once again.

No, it’s not because I’m indifferent to the approval of others, nor because the “like” button and the ★☆☆☆☆-★★★★★ rating system reduce the complexity of a human experience to a data point, nor because I’m ashamed not to be doing my share of (positive or negative) “like”-ing. If I have never “like”d anything online, nor given a star rating to anything, nor accepted the invitation to participate in a survey2 after an online interaction, it is because I consciously chose never to provide free labor for any platform, beyond what can unavoidably be deduced algorithmically from my decision to use the platform in the first place.

Much of Antonio Casilli’s Waiting for Robots is devoted to analyzing how internet platforms are structured in such a way that free users are simultaneously free laborers:

Because Facebook’s business model seems inseparable from the economy of click farming, we must subject its declared values of authenticity and autonomy to sharp scrutiny. The visibility market shatters the illusion of the user’s voluntary and carefree participation. New subscribers to social media are now caught up in a system of click production based on hidden work, including the “free” work they are asked to do, and the work done by their micropaid counterparts. The distinction between artificial and organic traffic has become blurred. Consequently, voluntary clicks by users on social media are of the same nature and are part of the same system of economic incentives, as those of individuals who are paid to circulate content, the only difference being that organic users are less costly for the platform. All users are workers. (Casilli)

As Casilli explains, this free labor includes the work of rating online purchases and customer service representatives (both human and artificial), the work of sharing travel stories on Twitter, the work of correcting Google translations and of posting photos on Google Maps, the work of solving reCapcha puzzles, and indeed the work of “liking” anything —notably posts on Substack, whose major investors include the billiard-ball headed billionaire bros already familiar to readers.

Substack is a platform like all the others, and today I am inviting readers to refrain from providing free labor for the platform’s investors by staying away from that little heart-shaped button.3

                                             Deskilling, not replacement

As this last quotation indicates, alongside the free labor provided by users one finds the paid, or rather micropaid, labor, whose role is also analyzed carefully by Casilli. It’s the latter kind of work, rather than that provided by users of social media and other platforms, that characterizes the participation by mathematicians in developing AI reasoning models for startups and hyperscalers in Silicon Valley and elsewhere. As I already argued in this earlier post, such work makes mathematicians “the functional equivalent for mathematical research of the Mechanical Turks.”

to a certain extent, the spread of subcontracting chains and the fragmentation of tasks on digital platforms points to a revival of the sweatshop system. (Casilli)

These two categories of workers — the users or subscribers and the Mechanical Turks —along with gig workers (who can also be read as “users” of platforms4 like Uber or Doordash) and others, provide the human labor without which AI is, on Casilli’s reading, even logically impossible. The following paragraphs, reached toward the end of Waiting for Robots, summarize Casilli’s primary thesis: that AI, like previous waves of automation, deskills rather than replaces labor.

Since machine learning only progresses if human data production increases, no truly autonomous machine can emerge that would dispense with human-treated input altogether. So if computing really does have a manifest destiny in the form of perfected artificial intelligence, it will also be irrevocably tied to digital labor. The Sisyphean task of machine learning has the following form: the more machine learning is applied to the automation of human work, the more it requires human work to feed it high-quality data.

The success of digital labor has thus been to transform work into a multiplicity of disparate tasks, but it has failed to create an autonomous intelligent system. This is due to a logical impossibility.… For the human intelligence that machines would ideally reproduce does not stand still.5 It adapts to new practices, and so any artificial replica must be constantly updated—a process in which, now as in the future, humans will be always involved.

Dallas Walker Smythe …introduced the concept of “audience commodity” to account for the activity of traditional media audiences.6 From his perspective, the time devoted to commercial media such as television and radio must be considered as working time when the attention devoted to the programs or associated ads proves to be fundamental to value creation. The capital circulates and accumulates by exploiting audience activity. Audience members aren’t simply consumers of cultural products. They are actually producers, not just of attention, but of “ideology and consciousness,” which makes of them service providers for advertisers and marketing professionals.… According to more recent research, audience labor extends to clicks, shares, comments, views, posts, status updates, and reach, all data that measure and organize visibility.7… digital labor, in addition to qualifying objects that are subsequently monetized in advertising, also involves performing human computational tasks from which value is extracted by the platforms for training algorithms and perfecting machine learning processes. (Casilli)

Subscribe now

                                                Mystification and gamification

There is a concerted effort among many tech leaders to basically create mystification around AI as a tactic, to a large extent, to disempower workers, policymakers, and anyone who might be critical of the growing concentration of funding and resources in our society toward this goal (Lisa Kresge, quoted in the Guardian, February 19, 2026)

While reading an electronic version of Casilli’s book I copied passages and pasted them into a file that now runs to over 11000 words. Many of these passages are specifically aimed at countering the mystification to which Lisa Kresge refers. Here are a few examples:

AI is not only produced in technological campuses outside rich cities in the US; it can also be found in cybercafes in Africa, in family homes in high-crime areas in South America, and in studio apartments in middle-class neighborhoods in Europe’s peripheries. Move away from the fantasy of the “entrepreneurial garage” that has dominated American startup culture for decades. Rather, picture a preindustrial cottage industry where AI is built by low-wage workers of all races and genders, not only by ambitious data scientists and software engineers. (Casilli)

The philosopher Ian Bogost … describes gamification as “exploitationware,” a program in which a worker’s effort is not elicited through direct and proportional rewards—a promotion or a salary increase, for example—but through opaque incentives such as stars, points, access to a new part of the platform, etc.8 (Casilli)

The productive effort of digital laborers is quantified through performance metrics (likes, scores, ratings, stars, and also the volume of followers, shares, and contacts), which are often associated with gamification (winning badges, goodies, triggering animated sequences in exchange for personal data and contributions), competition (comparing scores between different users of a platform to rank them according to their performance), or with self-assessment (activity reports, analysis of the most productive time slots, etc.). In fact, these are all control methods that are associated with a high level of technical subordination. … Panoptic surveillance gets completely reinvented with participatory surveillance. Digital labor ultimately establishes itself as “voluntary servitude” or “mandatory volunteerism” rather than as a way of emancipating workers. (Casilli)

                       Will the mathematicians of the future be venture laborers?

A recent Guardian article reports on a particularly ghoulish evolution in the Mechanical Turk model of AI training:

Gig AI trainers worldwide are selling moments of their lives, including calls and texts, to AI companies for quick cash.

One such trainer explains his thinking:

Ramelio Hill, an 18-year-old welding apprentice, made a couple hundred dollars by selling his private phone chats with friends and family to Neon Mobile, a conversational AI training platform that pays $0.50 per minute. For Hill, the calculation was simple: he figured tech companies already capture so much of his private data, so he might as well get a cut of the profit.

This is probably not an option for mathematicians working with the giant labs at DeepMind or OpenAI, or the specialized labs like Axiom or MathInc or Principia or the many others that are likely to spring up between the time I publish the post and the time you read it. But there is a version of the future in which mathematicians are not replaced but rather become indentured to the system, if not to a specific corporation. Here is a long quotation from Casilli that stretches the concept of “fair use.” I doubt that Casilli himself would object to sharing his ideas in this way, and I hope that his publisher (University of Chicago Press) doesn’t mind.

The fiction of platform work as path to worker emancipation ignores reality—workers lack choice. When confronted with the real working conditions of digital laborers, some theorists dismiss them—imagining their precarity and exploitation as anomalies that better training and minimal regulation can correct. … One thing that has been overlooked is that, if unrecognized digital laborers are subject to precarious working arrangements, this is because, over recent decades, recognized workers in the tech sector have set the example. Engineers, designers, and developers are all perceived to belong to the class of ‘innovative’ workers that embrace entrepreneurship. On-demand workers, microworkers, and moderators … are made to follow the example of their colleagues who are deemed to possess more skills and visibility.

Platform economies intensify pressures on “downstairs” workers to emulate the “upstairs” ones, but such pressures were actually developed already in the 1990s and early 2000s. Flexibility and job mobility have been a staple of tech work for decades. …the venture laborers of the dot-com boom … would move from one company to another, with periods of unpaid work, unemployment, and public subsidies. The phenomenon of venture labor, as defined by sociologist Gina Neff, “created a vicious cycle—taking risks seemed to be the only way to get ahead—encouraging entrepreneurial behavior from people in the industry, which in turn signaled to others that taking risks was a good idea.” Paradoxically, for these high-profile workers, career mobility and unpaid work were ways to deal with uncertainty. Workers could stay on top of the market by frequently changing jobs, building their portfolios, and working at big companies either for free or at a discount.…

The entrepreneurial spirit displayed by the recognized and visible tech workers is supposedly a link with their historical counterparts, the “exalted workers” of the Industrial Revolution. But is it true that underpaid and unpaid platform workers, like the elite ones of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, can choose their working conditions, their pay, and even the type of work they perform? Certainly, some workers in computer engineering, electronics, robotics, graphics, data science, and software development do have these choices. But, as we’ve seen, Amazon Turk’s microtaskers, Facebook’s moderators, and app-based delivery couriers all lack similar agency. (Casilli)

Where do mathematicians fit in this picture? Casilli explains how the status of “venture labor” deteriorated in the wake of competition from emerging economies that “employed innovative tech workers at lower cost.”

Suddenly, autonomy ceased to be a prerogative that these highly skilled workers enjoyed by default and instead became a problematic goal for them to strive toward. Working conditions deteriorated, and obvious forms of dependence on clients set in, which compromised their quest for emancipation. The image of a new generation of workers who are hyper-flexible of their own free will looked less and less credible. Flexibility, especially when it takes the form of moving between different projects or clients, does not imply that the workers concerned are managing their career paths as they wish. It is the companies, that is, the employers, who lead the dance. The flexibility and adaptability of workers, far from being signs of a new attitude toward work, are explicitly written into their contracts.

Now fast forward to today, and it is hardly surprising that the “exalted ones” themselves look more and more like microtaskers. This close connection between experts in digital services or freelance hackers, and clickworkers or on-demand platform workers becomes clearer when we discover that both categories are subject to the production chain constraints, controlled by digital platforms and large IT consulting and service outsourcing companies.

There is much more in this vein in Casilli’s book, which I recommend to everyone who harbors the illusion that AI, either on its own or as guided by its corporate owners, will eventually replace human beings in the practice of mathematics. What you won’t learn from Casilli’s book is what mathematicians will do to prevent an evolution into something that “look[s] more and more like microtaskers.”

                The 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians:  a clarification

Journalist Joseph Howlett asked me a few questions before he turned in his Scientific American article on the call to boycott this year’s ICM in Philadelphia. Here, more or less verbatim, is what I told him in response to one of his questions.

I think it’s evident to anyone outside the United States that holding the ICM in the United States, after it started two illegal wars, represents a double standard given that practically immediately after the after Russia invaded Ukraine, the ICM in Russia was canceled there.

This is not just what I think; by now more than 2000 colleagues have signed the boycott petition, and I’ve seen increasing repugnance internationally to the thought of coming to the US since Trump threatened that “a whole civilization will die” in Iran.

In the published article, the first words of the quotation were removed, so that it reads

“Holding the ICM in the United States, after it started two illegal wars, represents a double standard given that practically immediately after the after Russia invaded Ukraine, the ICM in Russia was canceled,” says Michael Harris.

The two sentences have very different meanings: what I actually said was an evaluation of a belief held by a large group of people concerned by the ICM, whereas the published version made this an expression of the personal opinion of a not particularly significant (or representative) individual. The change was made by the editors, not by Howlett, and I didn’t complain because what was published was not inaccurate, even though it wasn’t the point I was trying to make. I don’t think the change was made because the editors thought I’m poorly qualified to express judgments about what any large group of people believe. It’s most likely that the quotation was cut for the uninteresting reason that the article had to fit a strict word limit; somewhat less likely that the editor thought an unconditional expression of individual opinion looks livelier than burying an opinion in a dependent clause.

item.title: If mathematics is an art form, why don't we think like artists?
item.description: Thoughts on Molly Crabapple speaking at "A Night at the Library" in Brooklyn, followed by thoughts on the proposal to move the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians outside the US
item.dc:creator: Michael Harris
item.content:encoded:
It’s the things it’s doing right now…
                                            The greatest art heist in history

What was Molly Crabapple, the phenomenal and phenomenally prolific artist, writer, and activist, doing on the program of this year’s edition of Night in the Library, at the Central Branch of Brooklyn Public Library, co-sponsored by the Simons Foundation, scheduled on Pi Day, and devoted to the theme of Philosophy of Mathematics, when only a handful of mathematicians, and not even one actual philosopher of mathematics1, were listed on the program?

The talk was entitled Humans Against the Slopbeast. Let Crabapple explain in her own words:

Those too impatient to listen to the beginning of her talk can consult the online program:

Generative AI is a vampire, gobbling up more and more of our land, water, jobs, culture, and even our imaginations. How can we fight back against against this corporate colonization of our world?

Her main theme, established early on, is exactly what Melanie Mitchell said: it’s the things it’s doing right now that we should be worrying about.

Billions of images scraped from the internet and ingested by corporate plagiarism bots, stolen without credit, compensation, certainly not consent. It was the greatest art heist in history. Its purpose was to deskill, disempower, and replace us.…We artists were the canaries in the coal mine. It was us. Now it’s you.2

If Molly Crabapple is not aware that mathematicians are also in line for the industry’s deskilling, disempowerment, and replacement, by scraping billions of lines of “mathy data” from the internet, it is probably because no one among mathematicians is addressing the issue with as much eloquence and passion as she displayed in her Brooklyn talk. As I wrote nearly three years ago, upon listening to Tony Wu, then employed by Google, who at the time was busy scraping mathy data “without credit, compensation, certainly not consent” on Google’s behalf,

It is astonishing to me that the audience at Wu’s lecture was so detached from the circumstances of tech industry attempts to appropriate all human creation for its own commercial purposes … that no one raised the issue of copyright infringement at Wu’s talk.

                                               The rest of Molly Crabapple's talk

I started recording about half a minute into the talk. After five minutes I realized I could zoom in, so you can watch the next four minutes.3

To avoid saturating this post I recorded the last three minutes without video:

Just before the two-minute mark she alludes to Sam Altman, who “said that in the future, intelligence will be metered, like power, or water, and thinking will be centralized, and go through him.” As reported here as recently as the last post, mechanizing whatever he imagines mathematics to be is integral to Altman’s promised future.

Subscribe now

                   The unreasonable effectiveness of AI in undermining the ICM
Readers who have taken the trouble to listen to the first audio clip will have heard that Molly Crabapple altered her talk in response to current events:

That was the talk I had wanted to give. Then the US and Israel began this war with Iran.… U.S. bombs hit Shahal Sotun Palace. They smashed the tiles, they shattered the mirrors, they tore apart the wood panels and knocked the murals to the ground. Perhaps those bombs were targeted by AI. Maybe not.

Some readers may have strong feelings about this war. I certainly do. However, this Substack newsletter is only tangentially concerned with current political events, and those only insofar as I can claim they are connected, however loosely, to the mechanization of mathematics. So I have disabled comments for this post, because I don’t want to spend time moderating a discussion on this war, nor the previous one, nor the one before that, nor the war that our elected leaders have promised is on the way.

Instead, I would like to draw readers’ attention to this call to move the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians, scheduled for July in Philadelphia, out of the United States. Citing the decision in 2022 to move the ICM out of St. Petersburg after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the call asserts that

there is simply no sound argument one could make that claims international participants are more safe at this iteration of the ICM than they would have been in Russia in 2022.

On the contrary, the authors point to the following concerns to argue why international participants will not feel safe in Trump’s United States:

  • “mathematicians from all over the world… may not look to an ICE agent as though they ‘belong’”;

  • “the Trump administration’s …flagrant disregard of basic humanity all around the world” as evidenced by its kidnapping of the President of Venezuela, extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean, participation in the “ethnic cleansing of Gaza to make room for luxury real estate,” and of course the war in Iran.

They also mentioned the “absurd attempt to colonize Greenland completely against the desires of its current inhabitants.” I had already raised some of these issues in private conversations with mathematicians involved in planning the ICM. The consensus seemed to be that most international colleagues saw the operation in Venezuela as just another instance of the US doing its usual thing in Latin America, but that invasion of Greenland would be a step too far, and would definitely convince them to boycott the ICM in Philadelphia.

I am pleasantly surprised, therefore, to learn that, without waiting for a bloody action in Greenland, well over 1000 mathematicians (and counting) are already sufficiently outraged by the war in Iran to refuse to participate in a celebration of international mathematics just a few hours down the road from where that war is being designed and pursued. The list of signatories includes at least one whose participation is widely expected to be a highlight of the event. Since very few of those who signed the petition have shown any sympathy for the current Iranian regime, I suspect that the bombing of the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls’ elementary school and the killing of at least 170 people there on the very first day of the war may have helped to inspire the shared outrage on display in the call. Molly Crabapple speculated that AI may have been involved in the destruction of Shahal Sotun Palace. Two days earlier, 120 members of the US Congress had written to Pete Hegseth asking, among other things,

Was artificial intelligence, including the use of Maven Smart System, used to identify the Shajareh Tayyebeh school as a target?

That same day, James O’Donnell explained how this might work, concretely, in MIT Technology Review:

A recent conversation I had with a defense official suggests it might look something like this: A human analyst could put a list of potential targets into the AI model and ask it to analyze the information and prioritize which to strike first. The model could account for logistics information, like where particular planes or supplies are located. It could analyze lots of different inputs in the form of text, image, and video.

A human would then be responsible for manually checking these outputs, the official said. But that raises an obvious question: If a person is truly double-checking AI’s outputs, how is it speeding up targeting and strike decisions?

For years the military has been using another AI system, called Maven, which can handle things like automatically analyzing drone footage to identify possible targets. It’s likely that OpenAI’s models, like Anthropic’s Claude, will offer a conversational interface on top of that, allowing users to ask for interpretations of intelligence and recommendations for which targets to strike first.

It’s hard to overstate how new this is: AI has long done analysis for the military, drawing insights out of oceans of data. But using generative AI’s advice about which actions to take in the field is being tested in earnest for the first time in Iran.

“It’s the things it’s doing right now that we should be worrying about.” AI may not be threatening the future of human mathematics in quite the same way as “the greatest art heist in history” jeopardizes the livelihoods of artists “right now,” but the structural relation between the industry and the creative professionals is identical in the two cases. Two striking differences in the behavior of artists and mathematics, however, may help to answer the question in this week’s title.

The first is that the passivity of mathematics in the face of what could well constitute copyright infringement on the part of the generative AI industry is accompanied by a steady stream of reports of mathematicians joining the AI labs for what they mostly imagine (ignoring the warnings in this earlier post) will be a reversible phase transition. I assume — but I’m willing to be corrected — that nothing comparable is happening among artists.4

The second difference is that, however Silicon Valley hopes to cash in on the “greatest art heist in history,” it’s highly unlikely that the art works they have scraped are useful for developing systems for the identification of potential bombing targets, nor for the identification of potential targets for immigration agents. Mathematicians would be extremely naive to assume that their side arrangements with OpenAI or DeepMind or Anthropic — whose interest in mathematics is motivated by the goal of mechanizing human reasoning, and whose most generous long-term customers will be the government agencies responsible for war-making and surveillance5 — are not contributing to precisely the development of the concerns cited in the two bullet points above.

“It’s the things it’s doing right now…” At the end of Molly Crabapple’s talk I joined a line, waiting to speak to her to get her permission (which she graciously gave) to use the recording on this post. Just in front of me a math teacher was asking the speaker to help him sort out his misgivings about using the technology: he has found it tremendously helpful in enlivening his classes but he does not want to participate inadvertently in training commercial generative AI models, for all the reasons the speaker mentioned.

I would like to think that many of the signatories of the call are experiencing similar misgivings. A few months ago I was asked to join a panel on AI and mathematics at the ICM. In order to bring the spirit of this newsletter to Philadelphia, and to encourage colleagues to think critically about all the implications — starting with those highlighted by Molly Crabapple — of engaging with this technology and its corporate creators, I have not yet ruled this out. This is why I added my signature to a separate list at the bottom of the petition. But as the number of signatures breezes past 1100 this objective is looking harder to justify.
